prompt: During discovery for a new platform, a stakeholder states: *"The checkout API must respond in under 300 ms at the 99th percentile, and the system must remain available during a single-zone outage."* How should an architect classify these two statements?

choices.text: Both are functional requirements, because they describe what the checkout feature does
choices.rationale: Neither statement describes a feature or behavior such as placing an order. Both describe how well the checkout performs, so calling them functional confuses what the system does with how well it does it.

choices.text: Both are non-functional requirements, describing performance and availability quality attributes
choices.rationale: P99 latency is a performance attribute and surviving a zone outage is an availability attribute. Both are quality targets that can be expressed as user-facing indicators such as latency and request success ratio.

choices.text: The latency target is functional, because users see it, while availability is non-functional
choices.rationale: Visibility to users does not make a requirement functional. A latency threshold constrains how fast the feature responds, which is a quality attribute just like availability.

choices.text: Both are business requirements, too vague to be measured by any technical indicator, load test or probe
choices.rationale: Both are precisely measurable (milliseconds at a percentile, behavior under a zone failure), so they are technical, quantifiable targets rather than vague goals.

explanation: Separating functional from non-functional requirements is what lets you turn quality targets into SLIs and SLOs and pick an architecture that meets them.

prompt: A stateless web tier on Compute Engine must survive the loss of an entire zone with no manual intervention while keeping cost low. Which design best meets this requirement?

choices.text: A single large VM in one zone, protected by a daily snapshot schedule and a startup script
choices.rationale: One VM in one zone is a single point of failure. Snapshots help you recover the data but recovery needs manual action and takes time, so they are not high availability.

choices.text: A zonal managed instance group with autoscaling and autohealing in a single zone
choices.rationale: Autoscaling and autohealing handle instance failures, but a zonal MIG lives in one zone, so a zone outage takes the whole tier down.

choices.text: A regional MIG spread over three zones behind an external Application Load Balancer, with autohealing
choices.rationale: A regional MIG distributes instances across zones, so the surviving zones keep serving if one fails, autohealing replaces unhealthy instances, and the load balancer stops sending traffic to failed backends, with no manual step.

choices.text: Two unmanaged instances in different zones, with a DNS record changed by hand on failure
choices.rationale: Unmanaged groups have no autohealing, autoscaling or multi-zone management, and a manual DNS change means human intervention plus TTL delay before clients move.

prompt: An analytics team needs shared, POSIX-compliant file storage that multiple Compute Engine VMs and a GKE cluster can mount concurrently with low latency for a rendering workload. Which Google Cloud service fits best?

choices.text: A Cloud Storage bucket mounted on every VM and pod with Cloud Storage FUSE
choices.rationale: Cloud Storage FUSE is documented as not POSIX compliant: no hard links or file locking, whole-object writes, and much higher latency than a local file system.

choices.text: Filestore (for example the Zonal tier), mounted over NFS by the VMs and GKE pods
choices.rationale: Filestore is managed NFS with POSIX compliance, file locking and concurrent mounting from Compute Engine VMs and GKE clusters. The Zonal tier targets HPC, batch and media rendering.

choices.text: A standard Persistent Disk attached in read-write mode to a single Compute Engine VM
choices.rationale: A disk attaches read-write to one instance by default. Sharing is limited to read-only mode, or multi-writer on specific Hyperdisk types with a clustered file system, so it is not a shared NFS-style file system.

choices.text: A Cloud SQL instance with a shared schema that all rendering nodes read and write
choices.rationale: Cloud SQL is a relational database, so it stores rows rather than files and offers no file-system interface the rendering software could mount.

prompt: A team is building a new HTTP microservice that keeps no local state. They want to ship it as a container, have it drop to zero running instances when idle, be billed only while requests run, and avoid managing nodes or cluster upgrades. Which compute option best matches?

choices.text: Cloud Run, deploying the container as a service with the default minimum of zero instances
choices.rationale: Cloud Run is a fully managed platform for stateless containers: it removes the last instance when no requests arrive, bills per 100 ms of execution by default, and has no cluster to operate.

choices.text: GKE Standard with the cluster autoscaler and horizontal pod autoscaling both enabled on the cluster
choices.rationale: Standard clusters need nodes you manage and upgrade, and the autoscaler never automatically scales a Standard cluster to zero nodes because system Pods need at least one.

choices.text: A managed instance group of Spot VMs, each running the container under a startup script
choices.rationale: You still size, patch and run VMs, billing is for VM time rather than requests, and Spot VMs can be preempted at any time, which hurts a request-serving tier.

choices.text: App Engine flexible environment running the container on automatically scaled instances
choices.rationale: Flexible always keeps at least one instance running, so idle time is still billed. Scale to zero is a standard-environment feature.

explanation: Choose GKE instead when you need node-level control, DaemonSets, custom scheduling or complex multi-service orchestration.

prompt: A retailer is consolidating its product catalog and stock database. Stores on three continents write to it constantly, orders must see exactly one consistent view of stock, analysts query it with SQL, and write volume will keep growing. Which service is the best fit?

choices.text: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL scaled out with read replicas in each region
choices.rationale: Read replicas are read-only and asynchronous, and all writes go to a single primary, so write throughput cannot scale out across regions and remote reads can be stale.

choices.text: Cloud Spanner, adding nodes or processing units as write load grows
choices.rationale: Spanner is relational with SQL, scales horizontally by adding compute, and provides external consistency across multi-region configurations, which is what a globally written inventory needs.

choices.text: Cloud Bigtable, using a row key design that spreads writes across tablets
choices.rationale: Bigtable scales writes well, but it is a wide-column NoSQL store and replicated multi-cluster instances are eventually consistent by default. GoogleSQL queries do not make it a relational transactional database.

choices.text: Firestore in Datastore mode with multi-region replication
choices.rationale: Both Firestore modes are NoSQL document or entity databases, not relational SQL systems, so the analysts' SQL requirement and the relational stock model are not met.

prompt: A data-processing batch pipeline runs nightly, is fault-tolerant (tasks can be retried), and has no fixed completion deadline within the night window. Which two strategies most directly reduce compute cost while remaining appropriate for this workload? Choose two.

choices.text: Run the workers on Spot VMs, with idempotent, checkpointed tasks so preemption is harmless
choices.rationale: Spot VMs offer discounts of up to 91% and are documented as ideal for fault-tolerant batch jobs. Idempotent, checkpointed tasks mean a preempted worker just slows the job.

choices.text: Buy three-year committed use discounts sized to the peak nightly capacity of the pipeline
choices.rationale: A commitment bills monthly whether or not the capacity is used, so committing to peak capacity that runs a few hours a night pays for idle time.

choices.text: Use a managed instance group scaled by a schedule or queue metric down to zero between runs
choices.rationale: A MIG can be configured with a minimum of zero and scaled by a schedule or suitable monitoring metrics, so no VMs, and no compute charges, exist between nightly runs.

choices.text: Provision the largest available VM shapes and keep them running around the clock for headroom
choices.rationale: Idle, oversized, always-on machines are the opposite of cost optimization for a job that needs capacity only a few hours a night.

choices.text: Move the workload onto a multi-region Spanner instance to cut the compute bill
choices.rationale: Spanner is a relational database, not batch compute, so moving there does not reduce worker cost and adds expensive database capacity.

prompt: An enterprise wants its workloads to reach a Google Cloud managed service (and later a partner SaaS) using private IP addresses inside its own VPC, without exposing traffic to the public internet and without overlapping IP ranges with the producer. Which capability should the architect choose?

choices.text: Private Service Connect endpoints with internal IP addresses in the consumer VPC
choices.rationale: A PSC endpoint is an internal IP in your own VPC that maps to a Google API or a published service, including partner SaaS. It uses NAT, so consumer and producer ranges may overlap.

choices.text: Cloud NAT on the consumer subnets, so workloads reach the service through NAT IPs
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT gives outbound internet access to private resources. It sends traffic toward the public side, not through a private endpoint to a specific service.

choices.text: An external Application Load Balancer with Cloud Armor in front of the service
choices.rationale: An external load balancer exposes the service on a public frontend, which is the exposure the enterprise wants to avoid.

choices.text: VPC Network Peering with the producer's VPC, importing and exporting custom routes
choices.rationale: Peering requires non-overlapping subnet ranges and connects whole networks, not a single service, which fails the overlapping-range constraint.

prompt: A finance application has an RPO of 5 minutes and an RTO of 30 minutes. The team currently takes a nightly database export to Cloud Storage. What is the most accurate assessment?

choices.text: The nightly export satisfies both objectives, because it is stored durably in Cloud Storage
choices.rationale: Durable storage does not make the data fresh. The RPO is about how much data can be lost, and a nightly export loses up to a day.

choices.text: The nightly export violates the RPO, because up to about 24 hours of data could be lost
choices.rationale: RPO is the maximum acceptable length of time during which data might be lost. A failure just before the next export loses nearly 24 hours, far beyond 5 minutes, so continuous protection is needed.

choices.text: The nightly export misses the RTO but still meets the RPO, because restoring a dump is slow
choices.rationale: This inverts the metrics: the data-loss window of a nightly export is what breaks the 5-minute RPO, whatever the restore time turns out to be.

choices.text: RPO and RTO are interchangeable, so a single nightly backup covers both objectives
choices.rationale: RPO bounds data loss and RTO bounds downtime. They are distinct objectives, and a backup schedule addresses only the first.

prompt: An organization is planning a large migration and is classifying each application. One legacy app will be moved to Google Cloud as-is on VMs with minimal changes to hit an aggressive deadline, with modernization deferred. Which migration strategy does this represent?

choices.text: Rehost (lift and shift), moving the VMs as they are with minimal changes
choices.rationale: Rehost moves workloads with minor or no modifications. It is the quickest approach and defers optimization, which matches the aggressive deadline.

choices.text: Replatform (lift and optimize), swapping components for managed services during the move
choices.rationale: Replatform lifts the workload and then optimizes it for the cloud. That takes more effort than the as-is move the team wants.

choices.text: Refactor or re-architect the application into microservices before moving it
choices.rationale: Refactoring and re-architecting change how the code works, which takes longer and carries more risk than a deadline-driven move.

choices.text: Retire the application and decommission its servers without moving it
choices.rationale: Retiring means the app is no longer needed. The scenario says it will run on Google Cloud, so it is not being decommissioned.

prompt: Before migrating hundreds of on-premises servers, an architect needs to build an inventory, understand application dependencies, right-size target machine types, and produce a TCO estimate. Which Google Cloud tool is purpose-built for this discovery and assessment phase?

choices.text: Migration Center, with its asset discovery, fit assessment, dependency mapping and TCO reports
choices.rationale: Migration Center scans the on-premises estate for an inventory, identifies application and network dependencies, suggests Google Cloud targets from a fit assessment, and produces TCO reports.

choices.text: Cloud Deploy, with its delivery pipelines and release promotion across several targets
choices.rationale: Cloud Deploy is for continuous delivery of applications to runtimes. It does not inventory servers or estimate migration cost.

choices.text: Config Connector, with its Kubernetes-style manifests for Google Cloud resources
choices.rationale: Config Connector manages Google Cloud resources declaratively from Kubernetes. It does no discovery, dependency mapping or TCO analysis.

choices.text: Cloud Build, with its build triggers, test steps and container image build steps
choices.rationale: Cloud Build is a CI service that builds and tests artifacts. It has nothing to do with assessing on-premises servers.

prompt: An architect is reviewing a design against the Google Cloud Well-Architected Framework. The team proposes running every service across three multi-region deployments "to be safe," even for an internal tool used by 20 people during business hours. Which Well-Architected principle most directly challenges this proposal?

choices.text: Cost optimization: align resilience and spend with what the business actually needs
choices.rationale: The pillar says spending should align with business value and that you should provision only the resources you need. Triple multi-region for a 20-person, business-hours tool pays far more than it returns.

choices.text: Security: encrypt all data in transit between every pair of internal services
choices.rationale: Encryption in transit is a good control, but it does not address the issue here, which is paying for resilience the workload does not need.

choices.text: Operational excellence: automate every deployment with a CI/CD pipeline and IaC
choices.rationale: Automation is useful, but it does not question whether three multi-region deployments are warranted for this tool.

choices.text: Reliability: always maximize redundancy everywhere, regardless of the stated business need
choices.rationale: Reliability targets are set from what users and the business need, not by maximizing redundancy everywhere, so the pillar does not endorse this proposal.

prompt: A retailer is decoupling a monolith into services. They need (1) reliable asynchronous messaging to fan out order events to multiple downstream consumers, and (2) a managed way to run batch and streaming ETL pipelines. Which two services best address these needs respectively? Choose two.

choices.text: Pub/Sub topics with a separate subscription for each downstream consumer
choices.rationale: Pub/Sub decouples producers from consumers, and a message published to a topic is delivered to every attached subscription, which gives the fan-out.

choices.text: Dataflow, running managed Apache Beam pipelines for batch and streaming ETL
choices.rationale: Dataflow is a fully managed service for unified batch and stream processing, covering ETL and data movement with autoscaling.

choices.text: Cloud Interconnect circuits used to carry the order events between services
choices.rationale: Interconnect is dedicated hybrid network connectivity. It moves packets, it is not a messaging service with topics and subscriptions.

choices.text: Cloud CDN caching rules used to orchestrate the ETL stages at the edge
choices.rationale: Cloud CDN caches cacheable content at edge locations. It does not run or orchestrate data pipelines.

choices.text: Persistent Disk snapshots copied between zones to deliver events to consumers
choices.rationale: Snapshots are backups of disk contents, so they offer no event delivery, ordering or fan-out.

prompt: An architecture review team wants AI-powered help directly inside the Google Cloud console to investigate a cost spike, get design recommendations, and troubleshoot a misconfigured resource using natural language grounded in their own environment. Which capability is intended for this?

choices.text: Gemini Cloud Assist, working from the console with your project and organization context
choices.rationale: Gemini Cloud Assist is the AI collaborator in Google Cloud for designing and building, troubleshooting by analyzing logs and metrics, and cost optimization, grounded in your project and organization.

choices.text: Model Garden, browsing its catalog of models that can be deployed from the console
choices.rationale: Model Garden is where you explore, test and deploy models on the Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform. It is a model catalog, not an assistant for operating your own environment.

choices.text: Model Armor, screening prompts and responses for the questions the team asks in the console
choices.rationale: Model Armor screens LLM prompts and responses for risks such as prompt injection and sensitive data. It protects AI applications rather than helping architects with cost or design.

choices.text: AI Hypercomputer, using its integrated TPU and GPU supercomputing stack for AI workloads
choices.rationale: AI Hypercomputer is AI infrastructure for large-scale training and serving, with hardware, software and consumption models. It is not a natural-language assistant in the console.

prompt: Compliance requires retaining audit logs for 7 years. The logs are written once, almost never read (perhaps once a year for an audit), and must be retrievable within hours when needed. Which Cloud Storage class minimizes cost for this access pattern?

choices.text: Standard storage, keeping the logs immediately available at the highest at-rest price
choices.rationale: Standard suits frequently accessed data and has the highest at-rest cost, which is wasteful for logs read about once a year.

choices.text: Nearline storage, designed for objects read or modified about once a month
choices.rationale: Nearline targets roughly monthly access with a 30-day minimum duration, and its at-rest price is higher than Archive for data touched once a year.

choices.text: Archive storage, designed for data accessed less than once a year
choices.rationale: Archive is the lowest-cost class, has a 365-day minimum duration, and still serves data within milliseconds, so it fits seven-year logs read at most for annual audits.

choices.text: Multi-region Standard storage with object versioning enabled for audit safety
choices.rationale: Multi-region Standard with versioning raises both availability and cost, which works against minimizing the cost of rarely read data.

prompt: A migration business case claims success will be measured by "better performance." An architect is asked to make this a proper KPI. Which reformulation is the strongest KPI?

choices.text: The system will feel noticeably faster to users once the migration has completed
choices.rationale: "Feels faster" is subjective, has no baseline or threshold, and cannot be checked, so it cannot show whether the business case succeeded.

choices.text: Reduce p95 checkout latency from 1,200 ms to under 500 ms within 90 days of cutover
choices.rationale: It names a metric, a baseline, a target and a deadline tied to a user outcome, so it can be verified and linked to business value.

choices.text: The platform will run on the latest available generation of Compute Engine machine types
choices.rationale: Using new machine types is an activity, not an outcome. It does not show that users or the business benefited.

choices.text: The architecture will be improved by following Google Cloud best practices throughout
choices.rationale: Following best practices is an intention with no measurable target or deadline, so nobody can say whether it was met.

prompt: A healthcare provider runs a patient-records platform that must meet strict RPO/RTO targets and survive the loss of an entire region for its most critical write workloads, while controlling cost for less-critical reporting workloads. Which disaster-recovery approach best balances these needs?

choices.text: A single regional deployment for every workload, protected by Cloud Storage backups
choices.rationale: One region cannot survive a regional outage, and backup-based recovery cannot meet strict RPO and RTO for critical writes.

choices.text: Multi-region Spanner for the critical writes, with cheaper warm or cold backup-and-restore DR for reporting
choices.rationale: DR is tiered by criticality: the critical patient-records writes get multi-region replication and the 99.999% availability of multi-region Spanner, while reporting accepts slower, cheaper recovery.

choices.text: Active-active across three regions for every workload, regardless of how critical it is
choices.rationale: It would meet the targets, but hot redundancy for low-criticality reporting pays the highest standby cost for no business need.

choices.text: Everything stays on-premises, with snapshots replicated to Cloud Storage every night
choices.rationale: Nightly snapshots leave up to a day of data loss, failing the RPO, and the on-premises estate has no regional-failure protection of its own.

prompt: A global media company streams video and serves a web app to users on every continent. They need low-latency content delivery, a single global anycast entry point, and automatic routing of users to the nearest healthy backend. Which combination best meets these requirements?

choices.text: A regional external Application Load Balancer in one region, with Cloud NAT for egress
choices.rationale: A regional external ALB serves from a single region, so distant users get high latency and there is no cross-region failover.

choices.text: A global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN, and backends in several regions
choices.rationale: It exposes one anycast IP, terminates traffic near users, routes to the closest healthy backend with multi-region failover, and Cloud CDN caches content at the edge.

choices.text: One external IP per region published in DNS, with geo-routing maintained by hand
choices.rationale: DNS-based steering is coarse, depends on resolver caching and TTLs, and needs ongoing manual maintenance instead of automatic health-based routing.

choices.text: An internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in front of one regional managed instance group
choices.rationale: Internal passthrough Network Load Balancers are regional Layer 4 balancers for private traffic, so they cannot provide a global internet entry point.

prompt: An enterprise migrating Windows Server and SQL Server workloads to Compute Engine wants to control licensing cost and stay compliant. Which two statements reflect correct licensing planning on Google Cloud? Choose two.

choices.text: Pay-as-you-go premium images for Windows Server and SQL Server include the license in the hourly rate
choices.rationale: Premium images carry licenses billed by Google, which keeps new deployments compliant without separate license purchases. They cannot be combined with BYOL.

choices.text: Existing licenses that require dedicated physical cores can be brought to sole-tenant nodes
choices.rationale: Per-physical-core or per-processor licenses with dedicated hardware requirements need hardware, such as sole-tenant nodes, that is compliant with the license terms.

choices.text: Commercial OS and database licenses are free of charge on Compute Engine VMs
choices.rationale: Premium images include license charges in their price. The licenses are not free.

choices.text: Licensing has no effect on TCO, so it can be ignored during migration planning
choices.rationale: Licensing can be a significant part of total cost, and the choice between PAYG and BYOL changes both the cost and the hardware needed.

choices.text: Every license must be repurchased at full price whenever autoscaling adds a VM
choices.rationale: PAYG images are billed for the time the instance runs, so adding instances adds usage charges rather than new license purchases.

prompt: A retailer is rationalizing its application portfolio. One internal app duplicates functionality already provided by a fully managed SaaS the company now subscribes to, and it carries high maintenance cost with few users. Under a build/buy/modify/deprecate analysis, what is the most appropriate disposition?

choices.text: Refactor the application into microservices and run those microservices on GKE
choices.rationale: Refactoring spends engineering effort improving an application whose function is already provided elsewhere.

choices.text: Retire the application and move all of its users onto the SaaS product
choices.rationale: When a managed SaaS the company already pays for covers the capability, retiring the redundant app removes its maintenance cost and duplicate spend.

choices.text: Rehost the application unchanged on Compute Engine VMs and keep maintaining it
choices.rationale: Rehosting keeps the app running and still carrying its high maintenance cost, so it preserves the duplication.

choices.text: Rebuild the application from scratch on Cloud Run services and migrate its data
choices.rationale: Rebuilding invests the most effort in an app few people use and the SaaS product already replaces.

prompt: An automotive manufacturer is modernizing a complex platform with dozens of interdependent services that require custom networking, DaemonSets, a service mesh, GPU-accelerated inference, and fine-grained pod scheduling across hundreds of nodes. Which compute platform is the most appropriate primary choice?

choices.text: Cloud Run services for every component of the platform
choices.rationale: Cloud Run is serverless and removes cluster management, so node-level constructs such as DaemonSets and pod placement across node pools are not available. GPU support alone does not close that gap.

choices.text: GKE, with node pools, DaemonSets, custom networking and a service mesh
choices.rationale: GKE supports multiple node pools including GPUs, DaemonSets, custom networking configuration, and Cloud Service Mesh (formerly Anthos Service Mesh), giving the control this platform needs at the cost of more operations.

choices.text: One large Compute Engine VM running the services with Docker Compose
choices.rationale: A single VM offers no real orchestration, no scheduling across hundreds of nodes, and no high availability.

choices.text: App Engine standard environment with automatic scaling for each service
choices.rationale: App Engine standard is a managed application platform without node-level control, so it does not offer the scheduling, DaemonSets or mesh topology this platform requires.

prompt: Northwind Logistics has a predictable baseline of hourly spend across Compute Engine, Cloud Run, and GKE Autopilot. Over the next two years it will move VMs between machine families and shift some services between regions, so it cannot promise a fixed vCPU and memory shape. Which commitment approach captures savings while keeping that flexibility?

choices.text: Buy spend-based (flexible) commitments sized to the minimum hourly spend that is predictable across those services
choices.rationale: Spend-based commitments are denominated in dollars per hour and apply across several eligible services, so they survive machine-family changes and cover Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot as well as Compute Engine.

choices.text: Buy 3-year resource-based commitments sized to peak vCPU demand, so that no usage is ever billed at on-demand rates
choices.rationale: Sizing to peak guarantees paying for unused committed capacity during every trough, and a 3-year term maximizes lock-in exactly when the shape of the workload is expected to change.

choices.text: Buy resource-based commitments for the current vCPU and memory totals, scoped to the machine family in use today
choices.rationale: Resource-based commitments are tied to a region and resource type and cover Compute Engine only, so a family change or region shift strands the commitment and Cloud Run spend is never covered.

choices.text: Skip commitments and move every workload to Spot VMs, since interruptible capacity gives the deepest discount
choices.rationale: Spot VMs suit fault-tolerant work and cannot back steady, customer-facing services. Cloud Run and GKE Autopilot spend is also outside what Spot VMs would reduce.

explanation: Match the commitment type to how stable the shape of usage is: resource-based commitments suit known Compute Engine shapes, while spend-based commitments suit predictable dollar spend that spans services or changes shape. Commit only to the floor you are sure about.

prompt: Finance wants a monthly cloud-cost-per-order KPI broken down by product team, down to the individual VM or disk that drives the cost. All teams already apply a team label to their resources. What should the architect enable first?

choices.text: Pricing data export to BigQuery, so each team can multiply its own usage by the published SKU prices
choices.rationale: The pricing export lists prices and tiers, not what each team actually consumed, so the team would have to rebuild usage and credits by hand.

choices.text: A Cloud Monitoring dashboard of CPU utilization for every VM, grouped by the team label on each instance
choices.rationale: Utilization shows how busy resources are, not what they cost, so it cannot yield a cost-per-order figure.

choices.text: Detailed usage cost export from Cloud Billing to BigQuery, joined with order counts to compute the KPI
choices.rationale: The detailed export includes labels plus resource-level rows, so cost can be attributed to teams and drilled into specific VMs or disks and joined with business data in BigQuery.

choices.text: Per-project budgets with email alerts at 50, 90, and 100 percent of each team's monthly forecast
choices.rationale: Budgets warn about thresholds; they do not produce a queryable cost breakdown by label or resource and cannot be joined with order volume.

explanation: A KPI needs a numerator you can attribute and a denominator from the business. Billing export to BigQuery supplies the cost side at the grain you need; note that with a regional dataset the export starts from the day it is enabled, so turn it on early.

prompt: A video-sharing start-up stores 2 PB of user clips in one Cloud Storage bucket. Some clips go viral years after upload, so nobody can predict which objects will be read. The team wants lower storage cost without tuning rules per content type and without retrieval fees surprising them. Which design fits?

choices.text: Enable Autoclass on the bucket so objects move to colder classes when idle and return to Standard when read
choices.rationale: Autoclass transitions objects by observed access, returns an object to Standard when it is read, and has no retrieval or early deletion fees, which suits unknowable access patterns.

choices.text: Write all new uploads directly to Archive storage because it has the lowest cost per gigabyte stored each month
choices.rationale: Archive minimizes at-rest cost but carries high retrieval charges and a long minimum duration, which is wrong for clips that may suddenly be read heavily.

choices.text: Keep all objects in Standard storage and rely on Cloud CDN to absorb the cost of reads from older content
choices.rationale: Standard is the most expensive class at rest, and a CDN only reduces repeated reads of hot objects; it does nothing for 2 PB of idle data.

choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves every object to Coldline after 30 days, regardless of how it is accessed
choices.rationale: A fixed-age rule ignores access: a clip that goes viral at month 14 is served from Coldline and incurs retrieval fees plus minimum-duration charges.

explanation: Lifecycle rules encode what you already know about access; Autoclass is for when you do not. Autoclass keeps objects smaller than 128 KiB in Standard, which does not matter for video clips.

prompt: A bank keeps scanned loan documents in a regional Cloud Storage bucket. A new requirement says that after a full regional outage no more than 15 minutes of newly written objects may be unavailable, and applications must keep using the same bucket name with no failover code. Which design meets this?

choices.text: A multi-region bucket with turbo replication enabled so that both the location and the RPO are strengthened
choices.rationale: Turbo replication is available only for dual-region buckets, so it cannot be enabled on a multi-region bucket; default replication there has a much longer RPO.

choices.text: A dual-region bucket with turbo replication enabled, giving a 15-minute RPO under one bucket name
choices.rationale: Turbo replication targets replicating newly written objects across both regions within 15 minutes, and dual-region buckets keep serving from the available region under the same name.

choices.text: A regional bucket plus a nightly Storage Transfer Service job copying objects into a bucket in a second region
choices.rationale: A nightly copy gives a roughly 24-hour RPO and forces applications to switch to a different bucket name during an outage.

choices.text: A dual-region bucket with default replication, since dual-region buckets always replicate within a few minutes
choices.rationale: Default replication carries a 12-hour RPO even though most objects replicate sooner, so it does not provide the 15-minute guarantee.

explanation: RPO in Cloud Storage is a property of the location type and the replication mode: default dual-region and multi-region replication is 12 hours, and turbo replication (dual-region only) is 15 minutes.

prompt: The architect for a ticketing platform has set a checkout availability objective of 99.95%. The request path depends on the four components below, each of which must succeed for a checkout to complete. A reviewer claims the design meets the objective because the average of the component availabilities is 99.95%. How should the architect respond?

exhibit.label: Checkout request path and component availability
exhibit.content:
| Component | Availability |
|---|---|
| Global external Application Load Balancer | 99.99% |
| Regional GKE service (3 zones) | 99.95% |
| Cloud SQL (HA configuration) | 99.95% |
| Third-party payment API (no fallback) | 99.90% |

choices.text: Add a second Cloud SQL replica, because the database is the component that limits composite availability
choices.rationale: The database is not the limiting component; the 99.90% payment API is, and no amount of database redundancy raises that ceiling.

choices.text: Accept the claim, because the weakest component is only 0.05 points below target and rounding makes it equivalent
choices.rationale: The composite is lower than the weakest part, about 99.79%, so the gap is far larger than the weakest-link comparison suggests.

choices.text: Accept the claim: averaging is the standard way to combine component availabilities in a request path
choices.rationale: Averaging overstates availability. Every component in the path must be up for a checkout to succeed, so the failures compound rather than average out.

choices.text: Reject the claim: serial dependencies multiply to about 99.79%, so the payment API must be decoupled or the target revised
choices.rationale: Availability of hard serial dependencies is the product of the parts (0.9999 x 0.9995 x 0.9995 x 0.999 is about 99.79%), which sits below the weakest component and below the 99.95% objective.

explanation: Composite availability for a serial path is the product of the components: roughly 99.79% here. To reach 99.95% the payment dependency must stop being a hard dependency (queue and retry, degrade gracefully, add a second provider) or the objective must be renegotiated with the business.

prompt: Cymbal's suppliers drop product files onto an on-premises NFS file server, and brittle custom scripts copy them overnight for catalog enrichment. Cymbal wants a managed Google Cloud service to move these files into Cloud Storage on a recurring basis instead of maintaining scripts. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service as an agentless job pointed at the NFS path, because no software is needed on the premises side
choices.rationale: Agentless transfers apply to cloud sources such as Cloud Storage, S3, and Azure; file systems require agents and agent pools.

choices.text: Provision Cloud Interconnect so that the existing scripts can copy files into Cloud Storage over a dedicated private link
choices.rationale: Interconnect improves connectivity but leaves the brittle, self-managed copy scripts in place, which is the problem to solve.

choices.text: Order a Transfer Appliance and ship the supplier files to Google Cloud each night to avoid network use
choices.rationale: An appliance is for large one-time offline migrations, not for nightly recurring file drops that need to arrive in hours.

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service for file systems, with agents installed on on-premises machines that can read the NFS share
choices.rationale: File system sources are agent-based: agents in an agent pool run on-premises with access to the share and move data into Cloud Storage under a managed service.

explanation: Connectivity, transfer tooling, and orchestration are different layers. For recurring on-premises file movement the managed tool is Storage Transfer Service with agents; network links and appliances solve different problems.

prompt: A FinOps lead wants quick, low-risk savings from Google's built-in recommendations before the next planning cycle. Choose two actions that use native recommenders appropriately.

choices.text: Act on idle persistent disk recommendations, taking a snapshot before deleting any disk nobody uses
choices.rationale: The idle disk recommender flags unused disks and its guidance is to back up before removal, so deletion stays reversible.

choices.text: Buy a 3-year resource-based commitment equal to the current total of all running vCPUs across projects
choices.rationale: Current totals include the waste the recommenders are meant to remove, so committing to them locks in overspend for three years.

choices.text: Review VM machine type recommendations and resize instances that are consistently overprovisioned
choices.rationale: The VM machine type recommender suggests resizing based on observed usage, a direct way to cut spend without changing the workload.

choices.text: Disable autoscaling on all managed instance groups so spend becomes constant and easy to forecast
choices.rationale: Autoscaling reduces cost by matching capacity to demand; turning it off raises spend and does not use any recommendation.

choices.text: Delete every VM whose CPU stayed below 10 percent last month without asking the owner of each VM to confirm
choices.rationale: Low CPU does not mean a VM is unneeded; memory-bound, bursty, or standby machines look idle on CPU, so deletions need owner review.

explanation: Active Assist recommenders (machine type, idle VM, idle disk, idle IP, commitments) give evidence-based actions. Rightsize first, then commit to what remains.

prompt: A company has adopted a corporate sustainability goal. A new overnight analytics pipeline is not latency-sensitive and has no data residency restriction. Which approach best reflects how Google Cloud recommends using carbon data when choosing a region?

choices.text: Among regions meeting residency, latency, and price needs, prefer the highest carbon-free energy share
choices.rationale: Google's guidance is to pick a cleaner region for new applications and to run batch jobs in the cleanest option, while weighing residency, latency, redundancy, and price.

choices.text: Select the region with the lowest grid carbon intensity and ignore the carbon-free energy share it reports
choices.rationale: Grid intensity is a tie-breaker for regions with similar carbon-free energy percentages; the primary signal is the Google CFE share.

choices.text: Pick the region with the lowest hourly VM price, since carbon impact is the same in all Google Cloud regions
choices.rationale: Regions differ markedly in the share of carbon-free energy consumed, so carbon impact is not identical.

choices.text: Deploy the pipeline to every low-carbon region at once so that the workload always runs somewhere clean
choices.rationale: Running everywhere multiplies cost and data movement and does not follow any recommendation; one well-chosen region is sufficient for batch work.

explanation: Carbon-free energy percentage per region is one input alongside residency, latency, redundancy, and price. An organization policy with low-carbon location value groups can enforce the choice.

prompt: A customer-facing API runs on Cloud Run with request-based billing and scales to zero overnight. The first requests after quiet periods take about 4 seconds because of cold starts, against a p99 target of 800 ms. Traffic is modest, and the team wants to keep cost low. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Move the API to a GKE Standard cluster sized for peak traffic and keep the nodes running around the clock
choices.rationale: This removes cold starts but pays for always-on node capacity and adds cluster operations, which is out of proportion for modest traffic.

choices.text: Raise the maximum instances setting so that Cloud Run is allowed to start more containers during the quiet periods
choices.rationale: Maximum instances caps scale-out under load; it does not keep any instance warm, so cold starts after idle periods are unchanged.

choices.text: Set a small minimum number of instances, accepting the lower idle rate charged for warm instances under request-based billing
choices.rationale: Minimum instances keep containers warm so the first request does not wait for a cold start, and idle minimum instances bill at a reduced rate under request-based billing.

choices.text: Create a Cloud Scheduler job that calls the service every minute so that at least one container stays alive
choices.rationale: A ping is a fragile hack: it gives no guarantee of capacity, does not cover concurrent first requests, and bypasses the supported setting.

explanation: Cold starts are a minimum-instances problem. Google also recommends at least three minimum instances where high availability matters, and notes the minimum is a best-effort target.

prompt: An orders database runs on a single-zone Cloud SQL instance with a read replica in another zone. After a zonal outage last quarter, the business now requires automatic failover within about a minute, with no change to the application connection settings. Which change meets the requirement?

choices.text: Keep the existing read replica and promote it to primary whenever the monitoring system detects the outage
choices.rationale: Read replicas replicate asynchronously and have no automatic failover; promotion is a manual action and the application must be pointed at a new instance.

choices.text: Take on-demand backups every 15 minutes and restore the most recent one into the healthy zone after an outage
choices.rationale: A restore creates a new instance and takes far longer than a minute, and it loses everything written since the last backup.

choices.text: Scale the instance to a larger machine type with more memory so that it is less likely to fail during peaks
choices.rationale: A bigger machine changes capacity, not fault tolerance; a zone failure still takes the single instance down.

choices.text: Configure the instance for high availability so a standby in a second zone takes over using the same IP address
choices.rationale: HA keeps a synchronous standby in another zone; on failure the standby becomes primary in roughly a minute and clients reconnect through the same static IP.

explanation: Replicas scale reads and support manual disaster recovery; HA provides automatic same-IP failover to a standby in another zone. The standby does not serve reads.

prompt: A Spanner database on a regional instance holds a payments ledger. Two risks were raised: a faulty release can silently corrupt rows and may not be noticed for up to six hours, and an operator could accidentally drop the whole database. The database uses default settings. Choose two actions that address these risks.

choices.text: Switch the instance to a multi-region configuration so that every write is replicated to more locations
choices.rationale: Replication improves availability, but it faithfully copies a corrupting write to every replica and does not protect against dropping the database.

choices.text: Extend the version retention period beyond the six-hour detection window, within the maximum of seven days
choices.rationale: Version retention defaults to one hour, so recovery to a timestamp before the corruption is impossible after six hours; it can be extended up to seven days.

choices.text: Enable database deletion protection and tighten the IAM roles that allow dropping databases
choices.rationale: Point-in-time recovery does not cover deletion of the database itself; Google recommends deletion protection and restrictive IAM as additional safeguards.

choices.text: Rely on synchronous replication across the three zones as the recovery mechanism for logical corruption
choices.rationale: Zone replicas hold identical data, so they all contain the corrupt rows; replication is not a substitute for recovery to an earlier point in time.

choices.text: Keep the default one-hour retention, because point-in-time recovery also protects against deleting the database
choices.rationale: The default window is too short for a six-hour detection gap, and the documentation states point-in-time recovery does not protect against database deletion.

explanation: Logical corruption needs recovery to an earlier timestamp (version retention up to seven days); accidental database deletion needs preventive controls and backups. Replication addresses neither.

prompt: An IoT platform stores telemetry in a single-cluster Bigtable instance. The new requirement is to keep serving reads and writes if the cluster's zone fails, with failover that happens automatically and needs no application change, while tolerating briefly stale reads. What should the architect do?

choices.text: Add a cluster in another zone and send traffic through an app profile that uses multi-cluster routing
choices.rationale: With multi-cluster routing Bigtable handles failover automatically, sending traffic to the nearest available cluster; reads can be briefly stale until replication catches up.

choices.text: Add a second cluster and keep an app profile with single-cluster routing, then switch the profile if a zone fails
choices.rationale: Single-cluster routing sends all requests to one cluster, and failing over is a manual decision, which breaks the automatic, no-intervention requirement.

choices.text: Export the tables to Cloud Storage each hour and restore them into a new instance in another zone after an outage
choices.rationale: Hourly exports give an hour of potential data loss and a slow, manual restore, nothing like automatic failover.

choices.text: Add many more nodes to the existing cluster so that it can absorb the load if some of the nodes become unhealthy
choices.rationale: Extra nodes add throughput inside one zone; if the zone is lost, every node is lost with it.

explanation: Bigtable HA is a replication plus routing choice. Multi-cluster routing fails over automatically, while single-cluster routing preserves read-your-writes consistency but needs a human decision to fail over.

prompt: A shopping site keeps user sessions in Memorystore for Redis on the Basic tier. After a node failure, every user was logged out. The next design must survive a node failure without a full cache flush and must spread heavy read traffic. Choose two actions.

choices.text: Enable read replicas on the Standard tier instance so that read-heavy session lookups are distributed
choices.rationale: Standard tier can optionally enable read replicas, which distribute reads across nodes.

choices.text: Stay on Basic tier because it is intended for caches, so a full flush on node failure is the expected behavior
choices.rationale: Basic suits caches that tolerate a cold restart; sessions that must survive a failure are not that use case.

choices.text: Create a new Standard tier instance, which replicates to a replica and fails over automatically across zones
choices.rationale: Standard tier adds replication and automatic failover, so a primary failure does not flush the dataset the way a single Basic node does.

choices.text: Upgrade the existing Basic instance to Standard in place during the next maintenance window
choices.rationale: Tiers cannot be switched in place; moving between them requires a new instance and an import or export of the data.

choices.text: Stay on Basic tier and add a cron job that exports the data every hour to Cloud Storage as the backup
choices.rationale: Hourly exports mean sessions written since the last export are lost, and the instance still has no failover; users are logged out anyway.

explanation: Basic is a single node with cold restart on failure. Replication, automatic failover, and read replicas come with Standard, and migrating between tiers means a new instance.

prompt: EHR Healthcare must provide at least 99.9% availability for customer-facing systems. Its containerized patient portal runs on a zonal GKE Standard cluster with three nodes in one zone. Operations also report that the Kubernetes API is unreachable during control plane upgrades. Which redesign addresses both problems?

choices.text: Run a second zonal cluster in the same zone and split portal traffic evenly between the two clusters
choices.rationale: Both clusters share the same zone, so a zone outage still takes the entire portal down.

choices.text: Restrict upgrades to a maintenance window outside business hours while keeping the cluster zonal
choices.rationale: A window moves the interruption to another time but the control plane is still a single replica that is unavailable during the upgrade.

choices.text: Add more nodes to the existing zonal cluster so that the portal has spare capacity when individual nodes fail
choices.rationale: More nodes in one zone do not help when the zone fails, and the single control plane remains unavailable during its upgrades.

choices.text: Create a regional cluster, which replicates the control plane across zones and spreads nodes over three zones
choices.rationale: A regional cluster keeps the API available during upgrades and zone failures, and nodes in several zones keep serving if one zone is lost.

explanation: Regional clusters are the production default for availability. Budget for the node multiplication: a node count per zone is repeated in each of three zones, and cross-zone traffic is billed.

prompt: A hospital network needs 99.99% availability for its Dedicated Interconnect link to Google Cloud and wants the multi-region topology that survives the loss of an entire metro. Choose two requirements of that design.

choices.text: Provision two connections in one metro, one in each edge availability domain, since that already yields 99.99%
choices.rationale: Two connections in a single metro correspond to the lower 99.9% tier and do not survive the loss of that metro.

choices.text: Use regional dynamic routing so that each Cloud Router only advertises routes for its own region
choices.rationale: The multi-region topology needs global dynamic routing so that either region's attachments can carry traffic for the whole VPC network.

choices.text: Provision four connections in a single metro and place them all in the same edge availability domain
choices.rationale: Connections in one edge availability domain share maintenance and failure, so this gives neither the metro nor the domain diversity required.

choices.text: Provision at least four connections, two in each of two metros, spread across both edge availability domains in each metro
choices.rationale: The multi-region 99.99% topology requires at least four connections across two metros, distributed over both edge availability domains.

choices.text: Use global dynamic routing and create at least two VLAN attachments in each of two regions, with a Cloud Router per region
choices.rationale: The VPC network must use global dynamic routing, with at least four attachments across two regions (two per region) and a Cloud Router in each.

explanation: Interconnect availability SLAs are topology contracts: 99.9% needs redundant connections in one metro, and 99.99% needs four connections with metro and edge-domain diversity, plus matching attachments and routers.

prompt: A team is writing its first disaster recovery plan. Choose two statements that match Google Cloud's guidance on DR planning.

choices.text: The smaller the RTO and RPO values, the more the application costs to run, so targets should come from business impact
choices.rationale: Google's DR guidance states that tighter recovery objectives increase cost, which is why they should be tied to the business impact of downtime and data loss.

choices.text: Recovery procedures should be tested regularly, with automation and observability, to verify access paths and permissions
choices.rationale: A plan that is never exercised often fails on missing permissions or stale steps; regular, automated testing is part of the recommended approach.

choices.text: Having regular backups is sufficient because a DR plan consists of the backup schedule and its retention period
choices.rationale: Guidance says to plan end-to-end recovery beyond simple backups, including how systems are rebuilt, reconnected, and validated.

choices.text: RTO measures the maximum acceptable data loss, while RPO measures how long the application may stay offline
choices.rationale: The definitions are swapped: RTO is acceptable downtime and RPO is acceptable data loss measured in time.

choices.text: A hot standby is the cheapest DR pattern because the idle environment needs no resources until a disaster occurs
choices.rationale: Hot standby runs continuously and costs the most; cold standby is the low-cost pattern that is built after the incident.

explanation: Cold, warm, and hot patterns trade cost for recovery speed. Pick the pattern from the RTO and RPO the business needs, document end-to-end steps, and test them.

prompt: A script with an overly broad filter deleted objects from a production Cloud Storage bucket. The bucket uses default settings. The new requirement is that accidentally deleted objects stay recoverable for 30 days, and that regulated records cannot be deleted by anyone for one year. Choose two changes.

choices.text: Raise the soft delete retention duration on the bucket to 30 days, up from the default 7 days
choices.rationale: Soft delete keeps deleted objects recoverable for a configurable 7 to 90 days, and is enabled by default with 7 days.

choices.text: Apply a retention policy of one year to the bucket and lock it, so objects cannot be deleted before they expire
choices.rationale: A locked retention policy blocks deletion until each object's retention period expires, which is what a regulatory hold requires.

choices.text: Rely on the default settings, because soft delete retains deleted objects until an administrator purges them
choices.rationale: Soft-deleted objects are kept only for the configured duration, 7 days by default, after which they are permanently removed.

choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves objects to Archive storage immediately, since colder classes protect from deletion
choices.rationale: Storage class affects price and access, not whether an object can be deleted; Archive objects can be deleted like any other.

choices.text: Turn off soft delete to avoid paying for deleted bytes, and depend on object versioning for every deletion
choices.rationale: Soft delete is the recovery layer here; disabling it removes protection, and versioning alone does not stop a privileged user from deleting versions.

explanation: Recovery from mistakes (soft delete, versioning) and prevention of deletion (retention policy plus Bucket Lock) are different controls with different retention clocks. Soft-deleted data still accrues storage charges.

prompt: After a ransomware incident at another company, the board asks for assurance that Compute Engine and Cloud SQL backups survive even if an attacker takes over a project owner account and tries to delete them. Which design gives that assurance?

choices.text: Encrypt the backups with a customer-managed key in Cloud KMS and restrict who can use that key
choices.rationale: Encryption protects confidentiality; it does not prevent deletion of the backup resources or enforce a retention period.

choices.text: Keep snapshots in the same project as the workload and label them so that they are easy to find during recovery
choices.rationale: Labels aid discovery, not protection; an attacker with owner rights in that project can delete the snapshots along with the workload.

choices.text: Increase the snapshot schedule to every hour so that newer recovery points exist after an attack
choices.rationale: More frequent snapshots reduce potential data loss, but all of them remain deletable by the compromised account.

choices.text: Store backups in a Backup and DR backup vault with a locked minimum enforced retention period
choices.rationale: Backup vaults keep immutable, indelible backups; once the retention lock takes effect, no one, including project owners, can delete backups early or shorten the period.

explanation: Ransomware resilience is about backups that an attacker with admin credentials still cannot remove: isolation plus enforced, locked retention. Frequency and encryption are separate concerns.

prompt: A manufacturer runs a database on a Compute Engine VM in europe-west1 with a data disk and a separate log disk. The DR objective after a regional outage is an RPO of about one minute, in an active-passive pattern, with data that must remain on the same continent for regulatory reasons. Which design fits?

choices.text: Replicate both disks asynchronously to europe-west4 in a consistency group, with a runbook to attach the secondary disks
choices.rationale: Asynchronous replication targets about a one-minute RPO between regions on one continent, and a consistency group keeps related disks at the same point in time.

choices.text: Replicate both disks asynchronously to us-central1 so that the secondary copy is far from any European regional event
choices.rationale: Cross-continental replication is unsupported, and it would also move regulated data off the continent.

choices.text: Attach a regional persistent disk to the VM so that data is replicated synchronously across two zones of the same region
choices.rationale: Regional disks protect against a zone failure, not a full regional outage, so the DR objective is not met.

choices.text: Take hourly snapshots of both disks into a multi-region location and restore them in another region after any outage
choices.rationale: Hourly snapshots imply an RPO of up to an hour, and restore time adds to the outage.

explanation: Disk asynchronous replication is an active-passive regional DR tool: the one-minute RPO is a target (it can slip with high change rates), failover is a manual runbook, and both regions must be on the same continent.

prompt: A web tier on a regional managed instance group scales on CPU utilization. Each weekday shortly before 09:00 the load jumps sharply, and users see slow responses for several minutes while the group catches up. The pattern repeats daily and has done so for months. Based on the data below, which change best fixes the problem at reasonable cost?

exhibit.label: MIG autoscaler settings and weekday ramp (one-minute samples)
exhibit.content:
autoscaler: target CPU utilization 60%, min 10, max 60
instance initialization period: 240 s

time   requests/s  instances  p95 latency
08:55      800         10        180 ms
09:00    5,200         10      2,900 ms
09:02    5,200         14      2,400 ms
09:05    5,200         22        950 ms
09:08    5,200         34        210 ms

choices.text: Enable predictive autoscaling so instances are started ahead of the recurring daily ramp using the CPU signal
choices.rationale: Predictive autoscaling forecasts from history and starts instances before the load arrives, which helps most when initialization takes minutes and the pattern repeats daily.

choices.text: Raise the minimum group size to 34 instances so that capacity is always at the peak level from 09:08
choices.rationale: This fixes the symptom but pays for peak capacity around the clock, when only a short daily ramp needs it.

choices.text: Lower the CPU utilization target from 60% to 20% so that the autoscaler reacts to the ramp much earlier
choices.rationale: The autoscaler is still reactive and starts instances only after the load is present; a low target also runs extra instances all day.

choices.text: Increase the cool-down and initialization settings so that the autoscaler waits longer before it adds instances
choices.rationale: Waiting longer delays scale-out further and extends the period of degraded latency.

explanation: The evidence shows a reactive autoscaler losing roughly eight minutes: a 240 s initialization period and a step in load. Predictive autoscaling suits recurring, cyclical load and requires the CPU utilization signal; it does not predict one-time events.

prompt: A CPU-bound payments API runs on a GKE Standard cluster with a fixed replica count and a fixed-size node pool. During promotions latency climbs, and some new Pods stay Pending when nodes are full. Choose two changes that make the platform scale with demand.

choices.text: Also add a Vertical Pod Autoscaler on CPU for the same Deployment so that requests are adjusted continuously
choices.rationale: Google advises against using the horizontal and vertical Pod autoscalers together on CPU or memory because their decisions conflict.

choices.text: Rely only on the cluster autoscaler, since adding nodes automatically increases the number of replicas
choices.rationale: The cluster autoscaler reacts to unschedulable Pods; it does not create replicas, so the Deployment would stay at its fixed size.

choices.text: Raise the CPU limit on each container to a high value, so that a fixed number of Pods can absorb any spike
choices.rationale: Limits cap usage per Pod and do not add capacity; throttled or saturated Pods still serve slowly when traffic rises.

choices.text: Enable the cluster autoscaler on the node pool so that nodes are added when Pods cannot be scheduled
choices.rationale: The cluster autoscaler scales the number of nodes based on Pods that cannot be placed, which resolves Pending Pods.

choices.text: Add a Horizontal Pod Autoscaler on CPU utilization so that the number of replicas follows load
choices.rationale: The Horizontal Pod Autoscaler changes the number of Pods based on metrics such as CPU.

explanation: Pod-level autoscaling and node-level autoscaling are complementary layers: HPA adds replicas, and the cluster autoscaler adds nodes for the Pods that do not fit.

prompt: A billing pipeline consumes events from Pub/Sub. A subscriber bug once acknowledged messages after computing wrong taxes, and the error was found two days later. The design must allow reprocessing any message from the last three days without asking producers to resend. What should the architect implement?

choices.text: Retain acknowledged messages for at least three days and use seek to a timestamp to replay after a fix
choices.rationale: Seeking to a past timestamp replays acknowledged messages, but only if message retention is enabled on the topic or subscription beforehand.

choices.text: Set the acknowledgment deadline to three days so that messages stay available until downstream checks finish
choices.rationale: The acknowledgment deadline controls redelivery of unacked messages; it neither keeps acknowledged messages nor allows replay.

choices.text: Attach a dead-letter topic to the subscription so that wrongly processed messages are republished automatically
choices.rationale: A dead-letter topic receives messages that repeatedly fail delivery; messages that were acknowledged after a logic bug never reach it.

choices.text: Rely on exactly-once delivery, which guarantees that a processed message never needs to be handled a second time
choices.rationale: Exactly-once delivery prevents redelivery duplicates; it does not help when the code processed a message incorrectly and you need it again.

explanation: Replay is a design-time decision: enable message retention first, then seek by timestamp (or snapshot) when you need to reprocess. Without retention, acknowledged messages are gone.

prompt: An analyst deleted a table in a BigQuery dataset three days ago. The dataset uses default time travel settings, and no exports or table snapshots exist. What is the fastest supported way to get the data back?

choices.text: Open a support case to recover the table from fail-safe storage, which is the standard recovery path for deleted tables
choices.rationale: Fail-safe starts only after time travel expires and cannot be queried directly; using it requires contacting support, so it is not the first choice here.

choices.text: Query the table's metadata in INFORMATION_SCHEMA to read the rows, which stores a copy of every table's contents
choices.rationale: INFORMATION_SCHEMA exposes metadata about objects, not copies of table rows.

choices.text: Restore the table from its time travel history, since the default window of seven days still covers the deletion
choices.rationale: Time travel retains changed and deleted data for 7 days by default (configurable from 2 to 7), and deleted tables can be restored within that window.

choices.text: Re-run the upstream ingestion jobs from the source systems and rebuild the table from scratch over several days
choices.rationale: Rebuilding takes far longer and may be impossible if the source data has changed or aged out.

explanation: Time travel (2 to 7 days) is the first-line undo; fail-safe adds seven more days of emergency retention that only support can access. Longer retention needs table snapshots or exports.

prompt: Altostrat serves video segments through a global external Application Load Balancer with Cloud CDN in the default cache mode. After a redesign, origin bandwidth and latency rose sharply, and the cache hit ratio dropped to about 3%. Using the evidence below, which action is the most appropriate fix?

exhibit.label: CDN request log samples and origin response headers
exhibit.content:
GET /media/seg/ep4412/seg_0031.ts 200 cacheLookup=true cacheHit=false
GET /media/seg/ep4412/seg_0031.ts 200 cacheLookup=true cacheHit=false
GET /media/seg/ep4412/seg_0032.ts 200 cacheLookup=true cacheHit=false

origin response headers for /media/seg/ep4412/seg_0031.ts:
  Cache-Control: private, max-age=3600
  Set-Cookie: sid=9f31c0; Secure; HttpOnly
  Content-Type: video/MP2T
  Content-Length: 2104331

choices.text: Increase the default and maximum TTL values on the backend service so that cached segments live much longer
choices.rationale: TTLs only apply to cacheable responses; these segments are never stored, so longer TTLs change nothing.

choices.text: Add more backend instances at the origin so that cache misses are served faster during peak viewing hours
choices.rationale: This treats the symptom of misses by adding origin capacity, while every request still bypasses the cache and costs bandwidth.

choices.text: Change the origin so segment responses omit Set-Cookie and Cache-Control: private, since they make responses non-cacheable
choices.rationale: Responses with Set-Cookie or Cache-Control private or no-store are not cached; fixing the origin headers for shared static segments restores cacheability.

choices.text: Switch the cache mode to use origin headers only, so that the explicit max-age of 3600 seconds is honored
choices.rationale: That mode relies on valid origin directives, and the origin's private directive and cookie still make the response non-cacheable.

explanation: Read the evidence in order: lookups happen but never hit, and the origin sends Set-Cookie and private. Cacheability is decided by response headers before TTLs matter; segment content shared by all viewers should be served without session cookies.

prompt: A start-up offers a B2B reporting portal to customers located almost entirely in one country, served from a single Google Cloud region. It does not need a global anycast address, and it accepts somewhat higher and less predictable internet latency in exchange for lower networking cost. Which choice fits these requirements?

choices.text: Use Standard Network Service Tier with a regional external load balancer in the serving region
choices.rationale: Standard Tier costs less and routes over the public internet, and it supports regional load balancing, which is sufficient for a single-region audience.

choices.text: Use Standard Network Service Tier together with a global external Application Load Balancer for future growth
choices.rationale: Standard Tier is regional only, so a global load balancer with a single anycast address is not available in that tier.

choices.text: Keep the default Premium Tier with a global external load balancer, as Premium is always the better choice
choices.rationale: Premium carries a higher price for the Google backbone and global load balancing, capabilities this audience and latency tolerance do not need.

choices.text: Move the portal to on-premises hosting and connect customers over Cloud Interconnect to avoid internet costs
choices.rationale: Interconnect connects a customer's own network to Google Cloud; it is not a way for external users to reach a public portal more cheaply.

explanation: Premium Tier (default) uses Google's backbone and enables global load balancing; Standard Tier is cheaper, regional, and routes over the public internet. Choose it when audience and latency tolerance allow, which makes it a legitimate cost lever rather than a trap.

prompt: A transactional database on Compute Engine uses a 500 GB balanced Persistent Disk. Latency rises at peak. Using the evidence below, which change best fixes the bottleneck without paying for capacity that is not needed?

exhibit.label: Peak-hour metrics for the database VM and its data disk
exhibit.content:
VM vCPU utilization (p95):          22%
VM memory utilization (p95):        48%
Data disk capacity used:            41% of 500 GB
Data disk write ops throttled:      31% of requests
Data disk read ops throttled:       27% of requests
Database p99 query latency:         410 ms  (target 100 ms)

choices.text: Move the data disk to Hyperdisk Balanced and provision IOPS and throughput to match peak demand
choices.rationale: The disk is throttling while CPU, memory, and capacity are comfortable; Hyperdisk lets you provision performance independently of size.

choices.text: Place the database files on Local SSD, since it has the highest IOPS and is cheaper than provisioned disk
choices.rationale: Local SSD data does not survive VM stop or host events the way a persistent disk does, which makes it unsuitable as the only copy of a primary database.

choices.text: Move to a machine type with many more vCPUs so that the database has far more compute to process queries
choices.rationale: Processor utilization is only 22 percent; more compute does not remove the storage throttling that is causing latency.

choices.text: Resize the disk to several terabytes so that its size-linked performance limits rise above the observed demand
choices.rationale: Persistent Disk performance scales with size, so this can work but buys terabytes of unused capacity just to raise performance.

explanation: Diagnose from the evidence: low CPU and memory, ample free capacity, and throttled disk operations point at provisioned disk performance. Hyperdisk decouples IOPS and throughput from capacity so you pay for the performance you need.

prompt: A Cloud Run API holds a connection pool to a Cloud SQL database. During a promotion many requests were rejected with errors saying no instance was available. The team wants to serve the expected peak without overloading the database. Based on the evidence, which plan is most appropriate?

exhibit.label: Service configuration and peak-hour observations
exhibit.content:
# Cloud Run service
max-instances: 10
concurrency (per instance): 20
cpu: 1

# Observations at peak
concurrent requests arriving: ~900
container CPU utilization (p95) at concurrency 20: 58%
db connections held per instance: 8
Cloud SQL max_connections: 500

choices.text: Set minimum instances to 10 so that capacity is warm before the promotion and no requests are ever rejected
choices.rationale: Warm instances reduce cold starts but the 10 instances still cannot exceed the max-instances cap or the 200-request capacity.

choices.text: Raise concurrency from 20 to 90 and leave max-instances at 10, so that 10 instances can handle all 900 requests
choices.rationale: At 58% CPU with 20 concurrent requests, quadrupling concurrency would push each 1-vCPU instance well past saturation and raise latency.

choices.text: Remove the maximum instances limit entirely so that Cloud Run scales without any constraint during peaks
choices.rationale: Unlimited scale-out multiplies pooled connections and can exhaust Cloud SQL's connection limit, trading rejected requests for database failures.

choices.text: Raise max-instances to about 50 and keep concurrency near 20, since 50 instances hold 400 connections, under the limit
choices.rationale: Capacity is instances times concurrency: 10 x 20 = 200 is far below 900, while about 50 x 20 = 1,000 covers it, and 50 x 8 = 400 connections stays under 500.

explanation: Compute capacity as max-instances x concurrency (200 now against about 900 needed) and check what scaling out does to downstream limits: 50 instances x 8 connections = 400, below the 500 limit. Max-instances exists partly to protect backing services.

prompt: A retailer's flash sale will autoscale a new service from 200 to about 3,000 vCPUs in one region within an hour. The service is new, so there is no usage history. The team wants to avoid autoscaling failures caused by quota. Choose two actions.

choices.text: Wait for quota errors during the sale and open requests then, because exhausted quota refills automatically
choices.rationale: When quota is exhausted, work fails until capacity is freed or the limit is raised; it does not refill by itself.

choices.text: Borrow unused quota from an idle sibling project in the same organization during the sale
choices.rationale: Quotas are applied per project, and use in one project does not change another project's available quota.

choices.text: Count on the quota adjuster to raise limits automatically, since it works even for brand-new workloads
choices.rationale: The quota adjuster needs enough usage history to make predictions, which a new service does not have.

choices.text: Size the request against the regional quota, because usage in every zone of the region counts toward it
choices.rationale: Regional quotas apply across all zones, and zonal usage contributes to the regional total, so spreading across zones does not raise the ceiling.

choices.text: Request a regional CPU quota increase well before the sale, because approval is not guaranteed or instant
choices.rationale: Quota increases are evaluated by automated systems and carry no guarantee of approval or immediate provisioning, so requests must be made early.

explanation: Quota is a design input for scalability: plan peaks, request increases ahead of time, and remember regional scope. Autoscaling cannot exceed quota.

prompt: Altostrat's roadmap calls for Kubernetes environments both on-premises and in Google Cloud, managed with consistent configuration and policy from a central platform. Which Google Cloud capability should the architect build the future platform around?

choices.text: Merge all applications into a single namespace on one cluster so that there is only one configuration to manage
choices.rationale: A single namespace removes isolation and does not span on-premises and cloud environments; it is consolidation, not central management.

choices.text: Give every team its own cluster administrator with a separate copy of the deployment scripts for each cluster
choices.rationale: Per-cluster scripts recreate the drift and inconsistency a central platform is meant to remove.

choices.text: Connect the clusters with VPC Network Peering so that they automatically share configuration and policy
choices.rationale: Peering provides network routing between VPC networks, not shared Kubernetes configuration or policy.

choices.text: Register the clusters in a fleet and manage configuration and policy with Config Sync and Policy Controller
choices.rationale: A fleet logically groups clusters across environments and enables fleet-wide configuration, policy enforcement, and service mesh.

explanation: Fleets are the unit for multi-cluster management: sameness of namespaces and services, plus Config Sync, Policy Controller, and Cloud Service Mesh across clusters.

prompt: Cymbal's customer and catalog data sit in MySQL, SQL Server, and MongoDB, refreshed into analytics by nightly batch ETL, which leaves data silos and stale reports. As a forward-looking improvement, Cymbal wants a near-real-time unified view in BigQuery without running replication infrastructure. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Run the existing ETL scripts every five minutes on a larger VM to shorten the delay between systems
choices.rationale: More frequent batches add load on the sources and keep the custom scripts, failures, and maintenance that the service should remove.

choices.text: Migrate all three databases to a single Cloud Spanner database first and then build reports on top of it
choices.rationale: A big-bang consolidation delays the improvement for a long time, forces a schema and application rewrite, and is not required for analytics.

choices.text: Use Datastream to capture changes from the databases and replicate them continuously into BigQuery
