choices.rationale: Datastream is a serverless change data capture and replication service supporting MySQL, SQL Server, and MongoDB sources with BigQuery as a destination.

choices.text: Export each database nightly to files and load them with Transfer Appliance to refresh the warehouse
choices.rationale: An appliance is an offline bulk shipping method; nightly files are still batch and cannot give a near-real-time view.

explanation: Change data capture moves only changes, keeps analytics fresh, and avoids operating replication servers. Datastream sources include MySQL, SQL Server, Oracle, PostgreSQL, MongoDB, and Spanner.

prompt: EHR Healthcare wants to predict trends in claims and utilization from provider data already stored in BigQuery. The analytics team is strong in SQL and has no dedicated ML engineers. Which approach lets them deliver predictions soonest while keeping the data where it is?

choices.text: Build Looker Studio dashboards of historical totals and ask analysts to extrapolate the trend lines manually each month
choices.rationale: Dashboards describe past data; they do not generate predictions or forecasts.

choices.text: Use BigQuery ML to train and run models directly with SQL, such as time series forecasting, inside the warehouse
choices.rationale: BigQuery ML brings ML to the data, letting SQL-skilled analysts build models without moving data or writing Python or Java.

choices.text: Export the tables to Cloud Storage and train models on a self-managed GPU cluster run by a new platform team
choices.rationale: This moves data out of the warehouse and requires infrastructure and skills the team does not have, delaying delivery.

choices.text: Copy the data into a Cloud SQL instance and implement forecasting logic as stored procedures in the database
choices.rationale: Cloud SQL is a transactional database, not an ML platform, and copying data fragments the warehouse again.

explanation: Bring ML to the data when the data is already in BigQuery and the team's skills are SQL. Note that BigQuery ML availability depends on the pricing model: it is not part of the Standard edition.

prompt: Cymbal wants customers to find products by describing what they need in natural language, with personalized ranking, merchandising controls, and measurable conversion gains. The team prefers to buy rather than build commodity capabilities. Which direction should the architect propose?

choices.text: Run a self-managed Elasticsearch cluster on GKE and maintain synonym lists and ranking rules by hand daily
choices.rationale: This rebuilds a commodity capability, adds cluster operations, and offers no built-in personalization or retail-specific models.

choices.text: Extend the existing SQL queries with LIKE filters and extra indexes on the product name and category columns
choices.rationale: Keyword matching on relational columns cannot interpret natural language or personalize results, which is the current limitation.

choices.text: Train a recommendation model from scratch on GPUs and write a custom ranking service for the storefront
choices.rationale: Building from scratch demands scarce ML skills and long timelines for something a managed retail service already provides.

choices.text: Adopt Google's managed commerce search and recommendations service, ingesting the catalog and user events once
choices.rationale: The managed service provides search, recommendations, browse, and conversational filtering, with serving controls, personalization, and analytics export, using the same data for search and recommendations.

explanation: Cloud-first planning favors managed, domain-specific services over custom builds. The documentation currently names this product AI Commerce Search; Cymbal's case study refers to it as Discovery AI.

prompt: KnightMotives' supply chain runs on an outdated mainframe and a legacy ERP, which makes new dealer promotions hard to launch. A supply-chain outage would halt vehicle production, so leadership will only approve a path that proves the modernized system behaves like the old one under real production data before cutover. Which approach fits these conflicting goals?

choices.text: Leave the mainframe unchanged and build new promotion features as spreadsheets that dealers maintain locally for now
choices.rationale: This avoids migration risk but leaves the underlying constraint untouched and adds uncontrolled, error-prone processes.

choices.text: Retire the ERP immediately and recreate promotion logic in new services while the mainframe is switched off for good
choices.rationale: Switching off the systems of record before the replacement is proven creates exactly the outage risk leadership wants to avoid.

choices.text: Modernize incrementally, running the mainframe and the new cloud implementation in parallel and comparing results
choices.rationale: A parallel-run approach such as Dual Run validates functional equivalence on live workloads and limits disruption, supporting a phased transition.

choices.text: Automatically refactor the whole mainframe estate and cut over the whole supply chain during a single weekend window
choices.rationale: A big-bang cutover has no real-data validation period, which contradicts the requirement to prove equivalence before switching.

explanation: When the dominant constraint is risk, choose the migration pattern that lets old and new run side by side. Google Cloud's mainframe options include rehost, automated refactor, replatform, Dual Run parallel running, and Mainframe Connector for hybrid integration.

prompt: A data platform team pays unpredictable on-demand BigQuery charges because query load is spiky. Analysts also need to train models with BigQuery ML. Finance wants predictable cost without paying for peak capacity all month. Choose two actions.

choices.text: Buy a commitment sized only to the steady baseline of slots and let autoscaling cover the peaks above it
choices.rationale: Commitments discount capacity you will use constantly (20 percent for one year, 40 percent for three on these editions), while autoscaling avoids paying for peak all month.

choices.text: Size a 3-year commitment to the peak number of slots so that no query ever needs autoscaled capacity
choices.rationale: Committing to the peak pays for idle slots for most of the month and locks in cost for three years.

choices.text: Choose Standard edition to save money, since it includes BigQuery ML like every other edition at a lower slot price
choices.rationale: BigQuery ML is not available in the Standard edition, so the modeling requirement would not be met.

choices.text: Stay on on-demand pricing, because capacity pricing cannot autoscale and so always costs more for spiky load
choices.rationale: Editions support slot autoscaling and are billed by slot-hour, so spiky load can be served without paying for a fixed peak.

choices.text: Move to Enterprise edition with slot autoscaling, so that capacity grows for peaks and shrinks afterward
choices.rationale: Enterprise edition supports BigQuery ML and autoscaling slots, billed per slot-hour, which fits spiky load and the modeling requirement.

explanation: Editions turn BigQuery spend into capacity you can shape: commit to the floor, autoscale above it, and pick the edition for the features required (BigQuery ML starts at Enterprise).

prompt: A platform team spends much of its time tuning node pools and scheduling cluster upgrades. Its Pods typically request far less than the nodes provide, and the idle node capacity is a sizeable part of the bill. No workload needs special hardware. Which approach best aligns cost with what workloads use and reduces operations work?

choices.text: Move to GKE Autopilot, where Google manages the nodes and general-purpose Pods are billed on their requests
choices.rationale: Autopilot uses Pod-based billing for general-purpose workloads and removes node management, so idle node capacity is no longer a cost the team pays for.

choices.text: Stay on GKE Standard and switch to larger node machine types so that more Pods can be packed onto each node today
choices.rationale: Larger nodes still bill for the whole node, whether or not it is full, and the team keeps managing node pools and upgrades.

choices.text: Move the workloads to a managed instance group of VMs so that the team controls utilization of every machine
choices.rationale: That adds VM patching and orchestration work back to the team and removes the Kubernetes platform they already use.

choices.text: Stay on GKE Standard and enable only the cluster autoscaler, which removes the need to manage anything else
choices.rationale: The cluster autoscaler adjusts node counts but billing remains per node, and node pool and upgrade responsibilities remain.

explanation: Autopilot shifts billing from nodes to Pod requests (for general-purpose workloads) and hands node operations to Google; it is regional only. Workloads that need specific hardware are billed per node instead.

prompt: A SaaS company runs self-managed PostgreSQL on VMs. Heavy reporting queries slow down the transactional workload, and leadership wants a 99.99% availability target that includes maintenance, with minimal application changes. Choose two parts of a modernization plan.

choices.text: Keep the VMs, add more vCPUs, and build a manual standby copy that engineers promote during a failure
choices.rationale: This leaves failover manual and maintenance still disruptive, so it does not deliver the availability target.

choices.text: Migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL, which is PostgreSQL-compatible and offers a 99.99% SLA including maintenance
choices.rationale: AlloyDB keeps PostgreSQL client compatibility and provides a 99.99% availability SLA that includes maintenance.

choices.text: Add Memorystore in front of the database and drop the relational database from the reporting path entirely
choices.rationale: A cache accelerates repeated key lookups; it cannot answer ad hoc analytical queries over the full dataset.

choices.text: Rewrite the schema for Bigtable and replace the relational joins with application-side logic in every service
choices.rationale: A rewrite to a wide-column store breaks the requirement for minimal application change and removes relational capabilities.

choices.text: Use read pool instances and the columnar engine so that analytical queries run off the primary transactional path
choices.rationale: Read pools provide load-balanced read-only access, and the columnar engine accelerates analytical queries on live transactional data.

explanation: A modernization that preserves PostgreSQL compatibility lowers application risk, and separating analytical from transactional work addresses the performance symptom. AlloyDB also supports cross-region secondary clusters for DR.

prompt: An order-fulfillment process calls a payment API, an inventory service, and a third-party shipping SaaS in a defined order. It needs automatic retries with backoff, may wait hours for an external callback, and the business wants one place to see the process definition. Which service fits best?

choices.text: A Cloud CDN configuration that caches the responses of each API so that the process runs faster overall
choices.rationale: A CDN caches content for delivery; it does not coordinate multi-step business processes.

choices.text: Workflows, which orchestrates the calls in order with retries, callbacks, and a visible process definition
choices.rationale: Workflows runs steps in an order you define, retries HTTP calls with exponential backoff, supports callbacks, and acts as the canonical description of the process.

choices.text: A chain of Pub/Sub topics, where each service publishes an event that triggers the next service in line
choices.rationale: Event choreography spreads the process logic across services, so there is no single definition and ordering and waiting are harder to follow.

choices.text: Cloud Scheduler jobs that run every few minutes and call each service in turn using separate timed triggers
choices.rationale: Scheduled triggers poll on a clock rather than flowing from step to step, and they do not manage state, retries, or waiting for callbacks.

explanation: Use orchestration (Workflows) when you need explicit ordering, state, retries, and visibility; use events (Pub/Sub, Eventarc) for loosely coupled fan-out.

prompt: A payments ledger needs a 99.999% availability SLA and no data loss if an entire region becomes unavailable, with SQL and strong consistency. Which database configuration meets this?

choices.text: Spanner with a multi-region or dual-region instance configuration, which carries the 99.999% SLA
choices.rationale: Dual-region and multi-region Spanner configurations offer 99.999% availability, and dual-region configurations provide zero RPO during a regional outage.

choices.text: Bigtable with a single cluster in one zone and a nightly export of the tables to Cloud Storage
choices.rationale: A single cluster is a single zone, and nightly exports allow up to a day of data loss; Bigtable is also not a relational SQL ledger.

choices.text: Spanner with a regional instance configuration, whose replicas are spread across three zones of one region
choices.rationale: A regional configuration has a 99.99% SLA and cannot survive the loss of its region.

choices.text: Cloud SQL with high availability enabled and a standby replica in a second zone of the same region
choices.rationale: This tolerates a zone failure but not a regional outage, and does not carry the 99.999% SLA.

explanation: Spanner availability is chosen by instance configuration: regional is 99.99% and survives zone loss; dual-region and multi-region are 99.999% and survive region loss, at the cost of somewhat higher write latency.

prompt: EHR Healthcare must keep its legacy on-premises insurance integrations running for several years with no plan to upgrade them, yet it needs to onboard new insurers quickly and protect those backends from traffic spikes. Which forward-looking design reconciles these constraints?

choices.text: Rewrite the legacy file and API integrations right now, so that new insurers can connect to modernized services only
choices.rationale: This contradicts the stated plan to leave the legacy interfaces alone and delays onboarding until the rewrite finishes.

choices.text: Add Cloud NAT to the on-premises network so that every new insurer can reach the integration servers
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for private resources; it does not publish or protect inbound APIs.

choices.text: Place an API management layer such as Apigee in front, exposing modern, secured APIs with quotas and spike arrest
choices.rationale: API proxies form a facade in front of backends without changing them, adding authentication, quota and spike arrest, and analytics, and they let backends be replaced gradually behind the same API.

choices.text: Expose the legacy endpoints directly through an external load balancer so that new insurers connect to them
choices.rationale: Direct exposure adds no authentication, quota, or spike protection for backends that were never designed for internet traffic.

explanation: An API facade decouples consumers from legacy backends, so onboarding can proceed while modernization happens behind the facade, a strangler-style path to a cloud-first estate.

prompt: A pricing API behind an internal passthrough Network Load Balancer in us-east4 is consumed by on-premises systems through private DNS. A cheaper standby stack in us-central1 should receive traffic only if the primary is unhealthy, and the switch must happen without a human editing records. Which Cloud DNS configuration fits?

choices.text: A failover routing policy with a health-checked internal load balancer as active and the standby as backup
choices.rationale: Failover policies return the active set while it is healthy and switch to the backup set when all active addresses become unhealthy, with health checks supported for internal passthrough load balancers.

choices.text: A weighted round robin policy that sends half of the lookups to each stack, so that both always stay warm
choices.rationale: This sends half of normal traffic to the standby stack, which defeats the goal of using it only when the primary fails and raises its cost.

choices.text: A geolocation policy with geofencing that pins all on-premises clients to the us-east4 address
choices.rationale: Geofencing keeps traffic in the mapped geography even when the endpoints fail health checks, so it prevents the failover that is required.

choices.text: A single record with a very low TTL that the on-call engineer updates by hand when the alert fires
choices.rationale: That is a manual process dependent on a person and propagation time, which the requirements exclude.

explanation: Match the DNS routing policy to the intent: failover for active-backup, weighted for gradual shifts or active-active splits, geolocation for proximity or residency. Geofencing deliberately suppresses failover out of the geography.

prompt: A game studio runs a UDP-based matchmaking and voice service in a single region. The servers must see each player's original source IP address for abuse tracking, and the connection must not be terminated at a proxy. Which load balancer should the architect choose?

choices.text: Global external Application Load Balancer, because it offers one anycast address
choices.rationale: Application Load Balancers handle HTTP and HTTPS only, so a UDP voice and matchmaking protocol cannot be served by them.

choices.text: Global external proxy Network Load Balancer, which offers TCP with SSL offload
choices.rationale: Proxy load balancers terminate the client connection and do not preserve client IP addresses by default; this one is also TCP only.

choices.text: Regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer, which supports UDP traffic
choices.rationale: Passthrough Network Load Balancers support TCP, UDP and other IP protocols and are the type that preserves client packet information, including the source IP.

choices.text: Regional external Application Load Balancer, which can forward raw UDP datagrams
choices.rationale: Regional Application Load Balancers are still HTTP(S) proxies; they do not forward arbitrary UDP datagrams and would replace the client address.

explanation: Pick by protocol and by whether the source address must survive. Only passthrough Network Load Balancers handle UDP and preserve client packet information; Application and proxy load balancers terminate the connection.

prompt: A trading-analytics vendor exposes a custom binary protocol over TLS on TCP port 8443 to customers on three continents. The team wants one global anycast IP address, TLS termination at Google's edge, and backends in several regions with automatic routing to the nearest healthy region. Which design fits best?

choices.text: Global external proxy Network Load Balancer with SSL offload and backend services spanning multiple regions
choices.rationale: Correct: the global external proxy Network Load Balancer is the global option for non-HTTP TCP and the only type with optional SSL offload, with cross-region backends.

choices.text: Global external Application Load Balancer, since it is the only load balancer type with a global anycast address
choices.rationale: Application Load Balancers carry HTTP and HTTPS only. A custom binary protocol on port 8443 is not HTTP, and the proxy Network Load Balancer is also global.

choices.text: One regional external passthrough Network Load Balancer per region, with DNS geo-routing in front
choices.rationale: Passthrough balancers are regional and cannot offload TLS, and DNS-based steering is coarse and slow to react to failures compared with anycast routing.

choices.text: Internal Application Load Balancer with backends in several regions and a public DNS record
choices.rationale: Internal load balancers serve clients inside the VPC or connected networks and are not designed to be the internet-facing entry point for customers.

explanation: For non-HTTP TCP that needs a global entry point and TLS termination, the global external proxy Network Load Balancer is the match. Global Application Load Balancers are HTTP(S)-only.

prompt: Altostrat keeps its documentary and podcast library in Cloud Storage and wants to cut storage cost as volumes grow while every title stays available online. Access is unpredictable: an old documentary can go viral after years of silence, and many titles are never played again. Which approach best fits?

choices.text: Add a lifecycle rule that moves every object to Coldline after 30 days, since most titles stop being played
choices.rationale: A fixed age-based rule ignores re-access; titles that suddenly become popular would keep incurring retrieval charges from a cold class.

choices.text: Enable Autoclass on the library buckets so idle objects cool down and return to Standard when read
choices.rationale: Autoclass is intended for unknown or unpredictable access patterns: unused objects move to colder classes and any read moves an object back to Standard.

choices.text: Store the entire library in Archive and pay the retrieval charges whenever a title is played
choices.rationale: Archive is meant for data read less than once a year; frequently replayed titles would be dominated by retrieval fees.

choices.text: Keep everything in Standard in a multi-region bucket so that performance never varies
choices.rationale: This guarantees performance but ignores the stated goal of reducing storage cost for titles that are never played again.

explanation: When access patterns are unpredictable, Autoclass beats static lifecycle rules because it both cools unused objects and warms objects that are read again.

prompt: A logistics firm ingests tracker telemetry into Bigtable. After a traffic ramp-up, write latency degraded even though the cluster has ten nodes. Based on the exhibit, what is the most likely cause and the best remedy?

exhibit.label: Bigtable instance iot-telemetry, last 15 minutes
exhibit.content:
table: tracker_readings
row key format: <epoch_millis>#<device_id>
cluster nodes: 10
cluster write rate: 180,000 rows/s

node      cpu_util
node-1      96%
node-2       7%
node-3       8%
node-4       6%
node-5       7%
node-6       9%
node-7       6%
node-8       7%
node-9       8%
node-10      6%

write latency p99: 410 ms (was 8 ms before the ramp-up)

choices.text: Timestamp-leading keys funnel new writes into one tablet; lead with the device ID, then the timestamp
choices.rationale: The key starts with a timestamp, so consecutive writes land in the same key range on a single node. A high-cardinality prefix such as the device ID spreads writes across nodes.

choices.text: The cluster is undersized, so add more nodes until the busiest node falls below 70 percent CPU
choices.rationale: Only one node is hot while nine are nearly idle, so capacity is not the issue; extra nodes would not receive writes for the same hot key range.

choices.text: Add a second replicated cluster so that incoming writes are shared between both clusters
choices.rationale: Replication copies every write to both clusters; it does not spread a hot key range, so each cluster would develop the same hotspot.

choices.text: Pack each device's daily readings into one wide row to reduce the number of rows written
choices.rationale: Writing many cells into the same row concentrates even more load on one key, and rows have practical size limits, so this worsens the hotspot.

explanation: A skewed per-node CPU profile with a timestamp-first row key is the classic Bigtable hotspot. Fix the key design rather than adding capacity.

prompt: A smart-metering company ingests readings from 20 million meters at over a million writes per second and must serve the latest readings for a given meter in single-digit milliseconds. Queries are always by meter ID and time range, and there are no joins. Which database fits best?

choices.text: Bigtable, a wide-column store built for high-throughput, low-latency time-series data
choices.rationale: Bigtable targets time-series and IoT workloads with very high read and write throughput at low latency, scaling by adding nodes.

choices.text: BigQuery, because it scales to petabytes of time-series data and supports SQL
choices.rationale: BigQuery is an analytics warehouse; it is not the serving layer for single-digit-millisecond lookups on individual meters.

choices.text: Cloud SQL for PostgreSQL with time-partitioned tables to keep recent data fast
choices.rationale: A single-primary relational database cannot absorb over a million writes per second, and the workload needs no relational features.

choices.text: Firestore, because it autoscales and offers real-time listeners for changing documents
choices.rationale: Firestore suits document-centric app data with real-time sync, not sustained ingest of this scale for time-series keyed by device.

explanation: High-throughput time-series with key-and-range access and low-latency serving is Bigtable's sweet spot.

prompt: A SaaS vendor runs its order system on PostgreSQL. Product managers run heavy aggregate dashboards against the live data, and even with the queries moved to read replicas they take minutes. The team wants to stay PostgreSQL-compatible with minimal application change, keep dashboards on live data, and avoid building a separate warehouse. Which option fits best?

choices.text: Move the order tables to Bigtable and rewrite the dashboards around row-key range scans
choices.rationale: Bigtable is not PostgreSQL-compatible and would force a rewrite of both the application and the dashboards, contradicting the minimal-change goal.

choices.text: Add more read replicas, since each extra replica divides the aggregate scan time proportionally
choices.rationale: Replicas scale concurrency, not the speed of a single large scan, and the stem says the queries are already slow on replicas.

choices.text: Migrate to AlloyDB for PostgreSQL and use its columnar engine to speed up analytics on live data
choices.rationale: AlloyDB is PostgreSQL-compatible and targets mixed transactional and analytical workloads, with a columnar engine that speeds up analytical queries on live data.

choices.text: Replicate the data nightly into BigQuery and point the dashboards at that copy instead
choices.rationale: A nightly copy means the dashboards no longer show live data, and it adds the separate warehouse pipeline the team wants to avoid.

explanation: AlloyDB's HTAP positioning and columnar engine fit analytics on live PostgreSQL data without leaving the PostgreSQL ecosystem.

prompt: An insurer runs Cloud SQL for MySQL for its claims system. It needs automatic recovery from a zone failure within about a minute, and recovery from a full regional outage within an hour, accepting some data loss because replication is asynchronous. The solution must cost far less than a globally distributed database. Choose two.

choices.text: Rely on the high availability configuration alone, since its standby protects against a regional outage
choices.rationale: HA places the primary and standby in different zones of one region; it covers zonal failures and does not protect against a regional outage.

choices.text: Enable the regional high availability configuration so a standby in another zone takes over automatically
choices.rationale: HA gives automatic failover to a standby in a second zone, typically within about a minute of unavailability, covering the zone-failure requirement.

choices.text: Add a read replica in a second zone of the primary's region and treat it as the regional disaster plan
choices.rationale: A replica in the same region fails together with the region, so it does not meet the regional outage requirement.

choices.text: Create a cross-region read replica and promote it manually if the primary region is lost
choices.rationale: Cross-region replicas are the supported regional DR path for Cloud SQL; they are promoted manually, which fits the one-hour recovery objective.

choices.text: Send read traffic to the HA standby to offload the primary during normal operation
choices.rationale: The HA standby cannot serve read queries; only read replicas can.

explanation: Cloud SQL HA handles zone loss; regional loss needs a cross-region replica that is promoted manually. The standby is a failover resource only and cannot serve reads.

prompt: EHR Healthcare is moving its containerized customer-facing applications to GKE and must deliver at least 99.9 percent availability while keeping administration low. A team member proposes starting with a zonal Standard cluster in one zone and converting it to a regional cluster later if availability proves insufficient. What should the architect advise?

choices.text: Proceed, because a zonal cluster can be converted to a regional cluster with a single update command
choices.rationale: A zonal cluster cannot later become a regional one, so this migration path does not exist.

choices.text: Create regional clusters from the start, since zonal clusters cannot be converted later
choices.rationale: Google recommends regional clusters for production, and the cluster type cannot be changed after creation, so starting zonal would force a rebuild.

choices.text: Proceed, because spreading nodes across zones also makes the control plane highly available
choices.rationale: Node placement does not change the control plane: a zonal cluster has a single control plane in one zone, so configuration is unavailable if that zone fails.

choices.text: Proceed with one zone, because Kubernetes reschedules Pods into other zones when a zone is lost
choices.rationale: Rescheduling needs nodes in other zones; a cluster confined to one zone loses all of its workloads when that zone fails.

explanation: Cluster location is a creation-time decision: zonal cannot become regional. For production availability targets, choose regional from the start.

prompt: A security vendor's endpoint agent must run on every node as a privileged workload with host-level access, and the platform team also needs granular control over node pool settings. Which GKE mode should the architect choose?

choices.text: GKE Autopilot, because Google manages the nodes and permits privileged Pods by default
choices.rationale: Autopilot prevents privileged Pods as part of the best practices it enforces, so the agent could not run there.

choices.text: GKE Standard, because it supports privileged workloads and direct control of node pools
choices.rationale: Standard is the mode for workloads that need special privileges or granular control over node pools and node configuration.

choices.text: Cloud Run, because each container instance can be granted full host-level privileges
choices.rationale: Cloud Run is a serverless platform with no nodes to run a per-node agent on and no host-level access.

choices.text: Compute Engine managed instance groups, since GKE cannot run privileged containers at all
choices.rationale: GKE Standard can run privileged containers; the premise is false, and giving up Kubernetes would add operational burden.

explanation: Autopilot trades control for a managed, hardened node layer. When a workload needs privileged access or custom node settings, Standard is the right mode.

prompt: A platform team's GKE cluster stops scaling out and Pods stay Pending, as shown in the exhibit. They want to resolve the Pod address shortage without rebuilding the cluster. Choose two actions.

exhibit.label: Cluster prod-orders (VPC-native, Standard) configuration and autoscaler events
exhibit.content:
pod secondary range:        10.64.0.0/21
services secondary range:   10.64.8.0/22
node pool default-pool:     max-pods-per-node=110 (default), autoscaling 3-20 nodes
nodes ready:                8

12:01:07 cluster-autoscaler  scale-up requested: default-pool 8 -> 9
12:01:41 cluster-autoscaler  scale-up failed: no free Pod IP range available for a new node
12:02:10 scheduler           0/8 nodes available: Insufficient cpu. 14 Pods Pending
12:07:15 cluster-autoscaler  scale-up failed: no free Pod IP range available for a new node

choices.text: Add another Pod IPv4 range to the cluster using discontiguous multi-Pod CIDR
choices.rationale: GKE lets you add Pod IPv4 ranges to an existing cluster, which provides fresh address space for new nodes.

choices.text: Expand the primary IPv4 range of the subnet, because Pod addresses are carved from it
choices.rationale: Pods draw from secondary ranges used as alias IP ranges, not from the primary range, so growing the primary range does not help Pods.

choices.text: Add a node pool with a lower max Pods per node so each new node reserves less Pod space
choices.rationale: Reducing max Pods per node shrinks the block reserved per node, letting the same secondary range support more nodes.

choices.text: Add a Cloud NAT gateway so that Pods receive externally routable internet addresses
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT provides outbound internet access for private resources; it does not create Pod address space.

choices.text: Raise the autoscaler maximum from 20 to 40 nodes so more nodes can be created
choices.rationale: The autoscaler already tries to add nodes; the failure is address exhaustion, so a higher cap changes nothing.

explanation: With the default 110 Pods per node, each node reserves a /24 of Pod addresses, so a /21 secondary range supports only 8 nodes. Fix the address supply, not the node count limits.

prompt: A custom-mode subnet using 10.0.4.0/24 is nearly full and hosts production VMs that cannot be recreated. What is the supported way to add address capacity to this subnet?

choices.text: Replace the primary range with a new, non-overlapping CIDR block using a subnet update
choices.rationale: A subnet's primary range can be expanded but not replaced, so there is no in-place swap to a different block.

choices.text: Add a secondary range, which the VMs can then use for their primary network interfaces
choices.rationale: Secondary ranges are usable only by alias IP ranges; VM primary interfaces always take addresses from the primary range.

choices.text: Convert the network to auto mode, which resizes every subnet automatically as needed
choices.rationale: Auto mode creates fixed /20 subnets, and conversion goes only from auto to custom, never the other way.

choices.text: Expand the subnet's primary IPv4 range to a shorter prefix, such as /23, in place
choices.rationale: Primary ranges can be expanded in place without recreating resources, which fits VMs that cannot be rebuilt.

explanation: Subnet primary ranges can grow but never shrink or be swapped for a different range. Plan ranges with room to expand.

prompt: A company runs a hub VPC peered with spoke VPCs A and B in separate projects. Services in A must reach services in B, and more spokes are planned. The team assumes the hub will relay the traffic between its peers. Which change meets the need and scales to many VPCs?

choices.text: Attach every VPC as a spoke to a Network Connectivity Center hub, which provides connectivity between VPC spokes
choices.rationale: Network Connectivity Center offers hub-and-spoke connectivity among VPC spokes, which peering alone cannot do, and it scales as spokes are added.

choices.text: Keep the peerings; the hub relays routes, so traffic from A reaches B once the firewall rules allow it
choices.rationale: VPC Network Peering is not transitive: A and B are each peered with the hub but get no connectivity to each other through it.

choices.text: Add a Cloud NAT gateway in the hub VPC so that A and B can translate traffic through it
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT handles outbound translation to the internet; it does not create routes between peered VPC networks.

choices.text: Raise the peering quota for the hub so that it is allowed to relay between its peers
choices.rationale: Quotas limit the number of peerings, not their routing behavior; raising them does not make peering transitive.

explanation: Peering is point-to-point and non-transitive. For many-to-many VPC connectivity, use Network Connectivity Center spokes.

prompt: A company created an auto mode VPC network for a pilot. It now needs to connect the VPC to its data center over Cloud VPN, but the data center already uses 10.140.0.0/16, which sits inside the 10.128.0.0/9 block that auto mode uses for its subnets. What should the architect do?

choices.text: Keep auto mode and build the VPN anyway, since Google Cloud prefers the more specific on-premises route
choices.rationale: Using addresses inside 10.128.0.0/9 prevents connecting to an auto mode network over Cloud VPN, so the connection cannot simply be built.

choices.text: Convert the network to custom mode and put workloads in subnets that avoid on-premises addresses
choices.rationale: Custom mode gives full control of subnet ranges, which lets the team plan non-overlapping address space before connecting.

choices.text: Add a Cloud NAT gateway to translate the on-premises range into one that fits the auto mode block
choices.rationale: Cloud NAT translates outbound traffic to internet addresses; it does not solve address overlap across a VPN.

choices.text: Build the VPN first, then convert to custom mode later, since conversion can be reversed if conflicts appear
choices.rationale: Conversion from auto to custom mode is one-way, and it cannot be reversed to fix conflicts after the fact.

explanation: Auto mode is convenient for pilots but constrains addressing. Convert to custom mode (a one-way step) and design ranges that do not overlap with on-premises.

prompt: KnightMotives must upgrade connectivity between its manufacturing plants and Google Cloud. Several plants are far from any colocation facility where Google is present, and each needs a private link of roughly 500 Mbps to 2 Gbps, well below the capacity of a dedicated circuit. Which option fits best?

choices.text: Partner Interconnect through a supported service provider, with VLAN attachments sized per plant
choices.rationale: Partner Interconnect reaches Google through a service provider, with VLAN attachments from 50 Mbps up to 50 Gbps, matching a sub-10-Gbps need without a colocation presence.

choices.text: HA VPN only, because Interconnect is offered solely to customers inside Google colocation facilities
choices.rationale: Partner Interconnect exists specifically for sites that cannot reach Google's facilities directly, so the premise is false.

choices.text: Dedicated Interconnect with a 10 Gbps circuit per plant, since only that type carries a 99.99 percent SLA
choices.rationale: Cloud Interconnect SLA tiers depend on how the connection is configured for critical production, not on choosing the dedicated type.

choices.text: Dedicated Interconnect, because partners cannot offer attachments larger than 1 Gbps per site
choices.rationale: Partner attachments range up to 50 Gbps, and a dedicated circuit would be oversized and need a physical presence the plants lack.

explanation: When a site cannot reach a Google colocation facility and needs sub-10-Gbps capacity, Partner Interconnect is the fit.

prompt: A platform team is drafting hybrid connectivity standards for a bank. Which two statements about Cloud Interconnect are accurate? Choose two.

choices.text: To qualify for the 99.99 percent uptime SLA, the connection must be configured for critical production use
choices.rationale: Interconnect offers a 99.99 percent tier for critical production and a 99.9 percent tier for non-critical production; a connection with no stated reliability level has no SLA.

choices.text: Traffic is encrypted by default because Interconnect never touches the public internet
choices.rationale: Cloud Interconnect does not encrypt traffic by default; being private is not the same as being encrypted.

choices.text: Partner Interconnect VLAN attachments start at 1 Gbps and cannot be provisioned below that
choices.rationale: Partner attachments are available from 50 Mbps to 50 Gbps, depending on the partner and location.

choices.text: MACsec or HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect is needed when the link itself must be encrypted
choices.rationale: Because encryption is not on by default, organizations that need it add MACsec or run HA VPN over Cloud Interconnect.

choices.text: 100 Gbps connections are available at every colocation facility that supports Interconnect
choices.rationale: 100-Gbps connections are offered only at select colocation facilities.

explanation: Interconnect is private, not automatically encrypted, and its SLA depends on the topology and reliability level configured.

prompt: An internal HR portal serves employees in a single region, is not latency sensitive, and the owner wants the lowest network cost. Choose two design decisions that fit these requirements.

choices.text: Use a global external Application Load Balancer and run it on Standard Tier to cut cost
choices.rationale: Global external Application Load Balancers require Premium Tier, so this combination is not available.

choices.text: Select Standard Network Service Tier for the external IP address of the load balancer
choices.rationale: Standard Tier suits applications that are not latency or performance sensitive and can run within one region, at lower cost.

choices.text: Spread backends across two regions behind a Standard Tier address for resilience
choices.rationale: With Standard Tier all backends must be in the chosen region, so cross-region backends are not possible.

choices.text: Choose Premium Tier because Standard Tier cannot be used with external load balancers
choices.rationale: Regional external load balancers support both Premium and Standard Tier.

choices.text: Use a regional external Application Load Balancer with backends in that region
choices.rationale: Regional load balancers connect to backends in the same region only, and they support Standard Tier, matching a single-region audience.

explanation: Regional load balancer plus Standard Tier is the low-cost combination for single-region, latency-tolerant apps; global load balancing needs Premium Tier.

prompt: A team runs a self-managed PostgreSQL database on Compute Engine. If the VM's zone fails, a replacement VM in another zone must attach the same data volume without data loss. Which block storage choice supports this?

choices.text: Local SSD, which offers the highest performance of any storage choice available
choices.rationale: Local SSD data is lost when the VM stops or fails, so it cannot survive a zone failure.

choices.text: Regional Persistent Disk, which replicates data synchronously across zones
choices.rationale: Regional disks synchronously replicate across zones, so the data remains available to a VM in the other zone.

choices.text: A zonal Persistent Disk protected by a daily snapshot schedule in the same region
choices.rationale: A zonal disk is unavailable if its zone fails, and restoring from a daily snapshot loses up to a day of data.

choices.text: A Cloud Storage bucket mounted with Cloud Storage FUSE on the replacement VM
choices.rationale: Object storage mounted with FUSE is not a block device suited to a transactional database's I/O pattern.

explanation: Regional Persistent Disk provides synchronous cross-zone replication for block storage. Local SSD is ephemeral, and zonal disks share their zone's fate.

prompt: A Compute Engine OLTP database is I/O bound at its disk's IOPS ceiling, yet only 15 percent of the disk's capacity is used. The team wants more IOPS without paying for capacity it does not need and without redesigning the application. What should the architect recommend?

choices.text: Resize the existing Persistent Disk to several times its capacity so that its performance limit rises
choices.rationale: Persistent Disk performance scales with capacity, so this works technically, but it buys unused capacity, which the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Move the data to a Hyperdisk volume and raise its provisioned IOPS independently of its size
choices.rationale: Hyperdisk lets you configure performance and size independently, so IOPS can rise without adding capacity.

choices.text: Switch the data disk to Local SSD, which also keeps data when the VM is stopped
choices.rationale: Local SSD loses its data when the VM stops, suspends, restarts or fails, so it is unsafe as the primary store for a database.

choices.text: Attach a Filestore share and place the database files on it to gain additional throughput
choices.rationale: A network file share is not a drop-in replacement for block storage under an OLTP engine and adds latency and redesign risk.

explanation: Hyperdisk decouples provisioned performance from capacity; Persistent Disk ties them together.

prompt: An enterprise is lifting an in-memory SAP HANA database with a working set of about 8 TB onto Compute Engine. Which machine family category is the right starting point?

choices.text: Memory-optimized, which offers the highest memory-to-compute ratios
choices.rationale: Memory-optimized families are designed for in-memory databases such as SAP HANA, with very large memory capacities.

choices.text: Compute-optimized, which offers the highest per-core performance
choices.rationale: Compute-optimized machines target HPC and compute-intensive work, not very large memory footprints.

choices.text: General-purpose E2, which offers the lowest price for balanced workloads
choices.rationale: E2 is a cost-optimized general-purpose option for dev, test and modest workloads, with memory limits far below this requirement.

choices.text: Storage-optimized, which offers the highest block storage per vCPU
choices.rationale: Storage-optimized families focus on local storage throughput and capacity, not on maximizing memory.

explanation: Match the dominant resource to the family: memory for in-memory databases, compute for HPC, storage for local-SSD-heavy databases, accelerators for GPU workloads.

prompt: Cymbal runs containerized storefront services on self-managed Kubernetes clusters whose node patching and capacity planning consume engineer time, and one of its goals is cutting cost from manual processes. The services are ordinary stateless workloads that need no privileged Pods or custom node configuration. Which target is most appropriate?

choices.text: GKE Autopilot, where Google manages the nodes and applies security best practices by default
choices.rationale: Autopilot hands node management to Google and enforces best practices, which matches stateless workloads with no special node needs and the goal of removing manual work.

choices.text: GKE Standard with hand-tuned node pools, to retain full control over every node setting
choices.rationale: Standard's extra control is not needed here and keeps the node operations burden that the team wants to eliminate.

choices.text: Compute Engine VMs running a self-installed Kubernetes distribution in managed instance groups
choices.rationale: This keeps the team responsible for the control plane, upgrades and node lifecycle, which is the manual work they want to remove.

choices.text: GKE Standard with privileged mode enabled for all workloads, to keep maximum flexibility
choices.rationale: Enabling privileged mode widens the attack surface without a requirement for it, and still leaves node management to the team.

explanation: For ordinary stateless workloads, Autopilot reduces operations effort; keep Standard for cases that need privileged access or custom node control.

prompt: Altostrat analysts must query petabytes of viewing history with SQL for trend analysis, while the web app must fetch each listener's recent-activity profile in single-digit milliseconds at very high request rates. Which pairing of services fits best?

choices.text: Bigtable for the SQL trend analysis and BigQuery for the per-listener profile lookups
choices.rationale: This reverses the strengths of the two services: BigQuery is the analytics engine and Bigtable the low-latency serving store.

choices.text: Cloud SQL for both workloads, scaling the instance up as the history grows
choices.rationale: A single relational instance neither analyzes petabytes efficiently nor serves very high request rates at low latency.

choices.text: BigQuery for the SQL analysis and Bigtable for the low-latency profile lookups
choices.rationale: BigQuery is a serverless warehouse for petabyte-scale SQL analytics, and Bigtable serves high-throughput key lookups at low latency.

choices.text: Firestore for both workloads, because it scales automatically and supports queries
choices.rationale: Firestore suits document app data, not petabyte-scale SQL analytics, and it is a poor fit for this serving throughput.

explanation: Separate analytical and serving workloads: BigQuery for warehouse-scale SQL, Bigtable for single-digit-millisecond key lookups at scale.

prompt: A field-service app must keep working for technicians in areas with no signal, sync automatically when connectivity returns, and push live updates to dispatchers. The team wants automatic scaling with no database servers to size. Which database fits?

choices.text: Bigtable, which scales by adding nodes for sensor-style workloads
choices.rationale: Bigtable is built for high-throughput key-value data, with no offline client sync, and it requires choosing node counts.

choices.text: Firestore, a document database with offline support and real-time synchronization
choices.rationale: Firestore provides live sync, offline support for mobile and web, and automatic scaling without servers to size.

choices.text: Cloud SQL for MySQL, with an application layer that handles offline caching
choices.rationale: Cloud SQL needs instance sizing and has no built-in offline sync, so the team would have to build that layer.

choices.text: Spanner, which offers strong consistency and horizontal relational scale
choices.rationale: Spanner is a relational database with provisioned capacity and no offline client synchronization model.

explanation: Offline-first mobile sync with real-time listeners and serverless scaling is Firestore's niche.

prompt: A team is comparing Cloud Spanner instance configurations for a booking platform. Which two statements are accurate? Choose two.

choices.text: Regional configurations offer 99.99 percent availability; dual-region and multi-region offer 99.999 percent
choices.rationale: Spanner's published availability is 99.99 percent for regional and 99.999 percent for dual-region and multi-region configurations.

choices.text: Multi-region configurations lower write latency, because replicas sit near every writer
choices.rationale: Multi-region configurations add a small increase in write latency, since the read-write quorum spans regions.

choices.text: An instance's configuration is fixed at creation, so changing it requires exporting and re-importing the data
choices.rationale: An instance can be moved from one configuration to another without downtime, so no export and re-import is required.

choices.text: Multi-region configurations suit applications that read data from several geographic locations
choices.rationale: Multi-region is recommended when reads come from multiple locations or writes originate away from the reads, trading a small write-latency increase.

choices.text: Dual-region configurations are available in every Spanner edition, including the lowest tier
choices.rationale: Dual-region and multi-region configurations require the Enterprise Plus edition.

explanation: Regional covers 99.99 percent; dual-region and multi-region raise it to 99.999 percent with some write-latency cost and the highest edition requirement.

prompt: A fintech must keep all data within one country, serve users in that country from two regions, and meet a 99.999 percent availability target for a strongly consistent relational workload. Which design fits?

choices.text: Spanner regional configuration, which provides 99.99 percent availability within one region
choices.rationale: A regional configuration is one region and tops out at 99.99 percent, falling short of the target.

choices.text: Cloud SQL with high availability and a cross-region read replica promoted manually on failure
choices.rationale: Manual promotion with asynchronous replication cannot deliver a 99.999 percent availability target or horizontally scalable strong consistency.

choices.text: Spanner multi-region configuration with replicas spread across several continents
choices.rationale: Replicas spread across continents place data outside the country and add write latency.

choices.text: Spanner dual-region configuration with two regions in that country on Enterprise Plus
choices.rationale: Dual-region configurations serve reads from two regions in a single country, address data residency, and provide 99.999 percent availability.

explanation: Dual-region is Spanner's answer when residency confines data to one country but two regions and five-nines availability are required.

prompt: A broadcaster stores master video files in Cloud Storage and needs every new object replicated to a second region within 15 minutes, so a regional failure loses at most 15 minutes of uploads. Failover must be automatic with no application changes. Which bucket design meets this?

choices.text: A dual-region bucket with turbo replication enabled for all newly written objects
choices.rationale: Turbo replication targets replication within 15 minutes for dual-region buckets, and dual-region failover is automatic.

choices.text: A multi-region bucket, relying on its default replication to meet the 15 minutes
choices.rationale: Turbo replication applies specifically to dual-region buckets; multi-region replication is asynchronous without that 15-minute target.

choices.text: A single-region bucket plus a nightly Storage Transfer Service copy to another region
choices.rationale: A nightly copy implies up to a day of exposure, far beyond the 15-minute objective.

choices.text: A single-region bucket with Autoclass enabled to improve its resilience
choices.rationale: Autoclass manages storage classes by access pattern and has no effect on cross-region replication.

explanation: For a tight cross-region RPO on object data, choose dual-region with turbo replication.

prompt: A company must rehost 400 VMware vSphere virtual machines onto Compute Engine with minimal changes, using continuous replication and the ability to validate each VM before cutover. Which Google Cloud service is designed for this?

choices.text: Migrate to Containers, which converts VM workloads into container images
choices.rationale: Migrate to Containers modernizes workloads into containers for GKE or Cloud Run; it is a replatforming tool, not a VM-to-VM rehost.

choices.text: Database Migration Service, which replicates databases into managed Cloud SQL engines
choices.rationale: It migrates databases into Cloud SQL or AlloyDB, not whole virtual machines.

choices.text: Migrate to Virtual Machines, which moves vSphere, AWS and Azure VMs to Compute Engine
choices.rationale: Migrate to Virtual Machines migrates VMs from vSphere, AWS, Azure and VMware Engine to Compute Engine with replication and test-clones.

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service, which moves object and file data into Cloud Storage
choices.rationale: It moves data into Cloud Storage and does not replicate whole machines or create Compute Engine instances.

explanation: Pick the tool by what is being moved: VMs (Migrate to Virtual Machines), databases (Database Migration Service), files and objects (Storage Transfer Service), or VM-to-container modernization (Migrate to Containers).

prompt: A team has finished the initial replication of a VM with Migrate to Virtual Machines. They want to confirm the application boots and passes smoke tests on Compute Engine without any outage for the source VM. What should they do next?

choices.text: Run a cut-over, then power the source VM back on if the smoke tests fail afterwards
choices.rationale: A cut-over stops the source VM and completes a final replication, which causes the very outage the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Stop the source VM so that the test works against a quiescent final copy of its data
choices.rationale: Stopping the source VM causes an outage, and a test-clone does not require it.

choices.text: Run finalize to confirm that the replicated data is consistent before the testing begins
choices.rationale: Finalize deletes all replication data after a successful cut-over, so it would destroy the data being tested.

choices.text: Create a test-clone from replication data and validate it while replication continues
choices.rationale: A test-clone is a snapshot created from replication data; the source VM keeps running and replication continues in the background.

explanation: Test-clones validate the target without touching the source. Cut-over stops the source; finalize deletes replication data.

prompt: Two hours after cutting over an order-management VM with Migrate to Virtual Machines, a team finds a licensing failure and decides to return to the original VM. During those two hours the migrated VM accepted new orders. Which two actions belong in the rollback plan? Choose two.

choices.text: Run finalize so that the source VM is restored from the replication data
choices.rationale: Finalize deletes the replication data and other storage for the migrated VM; it does not restore anything.

choices.text: Rely on the service's automated rollback to replay the new orders into the source VM
choices.rationale: Rollback is not an automated process, and data written to the migrated instance is not synchronized back to the source.

choices.text: Plan a manual reconciliation of the orders written to the migrated VM after cutover
choices.rationale: Writes made on the migrated instance are not synchronized back to the source, so the team must reconcile them explicitly.

choices.text: Create a test-clone from the replication data, which reverts the cut-over
choices.rationale: A test-clone is a separate static snapshot used for validation; it does not undo a cut-over.

choices.text: Delete the migrated Compute Engine VM and start the source VM again
choices.rationale: Returning to the source means deleting the Compute Engine VM and restarting the original, which was stopped during cut-over.

explanation: Rollback after cut-over is manual: restart the source and reconcile any data written in the meantime. That is why finalize should wait until validation is complete.

prompt: EHR Healthcare is moving its billing MySQL database to Cloud SQL with a continuous Database Migration Service job. The cutover window has opened and the exhibit shows the latest job status. What should the engineer do before promoting the destination?

exhibit.label: Migration job ehr-billing-mysql (continuous), status history
exhibit.content:
time    phase            replication_delay    source accepting writes
09:00   full dump        n/a                  yes
10:30   CDC              2,460 s              yes
11:30   CDC                310 s              yes
12:15   CDC                 18 s              yes
12:20   CDC                  4 s              yes
12:25   CDC                  0 s              yes (billing app still connected)

cutover window: opens 12:25

choices.text: Promote now, because a replication delay of zero proves that nothing further can arrive
choices.rationale: The delay is zero only at this instant while the application is still writing, so new changes can still arrive after promotion.

choices.text: Promote now and stop the application afterwards, since remaining changes drain after promotion
choices.rationale: Writes must be stopped before promotion; changes made after promotion are not carried over.

choices.text: Stop writes at the source, confirm the replication delay stays at zero, then promote the destination
choices.rationale: The documented cutover sequence is to stop all writes, wait for the replication delay to reach zero, then promote.

choices.text: Delete the migration job first so that the destination detaches cleanly, then repoint the application
choices.rationale: Deleting the job removes the replication that keeps the destination current and skips the promotion step.

explanation: A zero lag reading with live writes is a moment, not a guarantee. Quiesce the source, confirm lag stays at zero, then promote.

prompt: A logistics firm will move a 2 TB Oracle database to PostgreSQL on Google Cloud with minimal downtime. The schema and stored procedures must be converted, and the source stays online during migration. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Use Database Migration Service heterogeneous migration: conversion workspace, then a continuous job
choices.rationale: Heterogeneous migrations use conversion workspaces to convert schema and code, and continuous jobs keep the destination current while the source stays online.

choices.text: Run a Database Migration Service job that copies rows between the two engines as-is, with no conversion
choices.rationale: Moving between different engines requires schema and code conversion; the service does that through a conversion workspace, not as-is copying.

choices.text: Use Storage Transfer Service to copy the Oracle data files to Cloud Storage and attach them to Cloud SQL
choices.rationale: Storage Transfer Service moves files; Oracle data files cannot be attached to a PostgreSQL engine.

choices.text: Use Datastream to stream changes into BigQuery, then export the tables into PostgreSQL after cutover
choices.rationale: Datastream targets analytics replication, not schema and procedure conversion, and a BigQuery detour adds risk and downtime.

explanation: Different engines mean a heterogeneous migration: convert schema and code in a conversion workspace, then replicate continuously and cut over.

prompt: Cymbal needs changes from its operational MySQL catalog and customer databases to appear in BigQuery within minutes to build a unified customer view. The storefront keeps using the source databases, and the team does not want to run replication servers. Which service fits?

choices.text: Database Migration Service, promoting each destination as the new primary
choices.rationale: Promotion turns a destination into the primary database for cutover; it is a migration step, not ongoing analytics replication.

choices.text: Scheduled BigQuery exports run against each database every night at midnight
choices.rationale: Nightly exports cannot meet a within-minutes freshness requirement and need custom scripting.

choices.text: Datastream, a serverless CDC service that replicates changes into BigQuery
choices.rationale: Datastream is serverless CDC and replication with minimal latency from sources such as MySQL into BigQuery, with no infrastructure to manage.

choices.text: Transfer Appliance, shipping periodic snapshots of each database to Google
choices.rationale: Offline shipping suits bulk one-time moves and cannot provide continuous changes within minutes.

explanation: For near-real-time database-to-BigQuery replication without servers to run, use Datastream. Database Migration Service is for moving the database itself.

prompt: A company must move data from three sites to Cloud Storage. Assume each link sustains about half of its rated speed, and use the guidance that an appliance is worth considering when an online upload would take more than a week. Based on the exhibit, which plan is best?

exhibit.label: Data migration inventory
exhibit.content:
| Site | Data to move | Usable uplink (rated) |
|---|---|---|
| A - Lisbon | 2 TB | 1 Gbps |
| B - Austin | 600 TB | 200 Mbps |
| C - Osaka | 40 TB | 10 Gbps (Cloud Interconnect) |

choices.text: Transfer Appliance at all three sites, so that one consistent method is used throughout
choices.rationale: Sites A and C would finish online in about a day, well under a week, so shipping appliances there adds cost and delay.

choices.text: Transfer Appliance for Sites A and B, and online transfer for Site C because it has Interconnect
choices.rationale: Site A holds only 2 TB on a 1 Gbps link and takes hours online, so an appliance is unnecessary there.

choices.text: Online transfer for all three sites, using Storage Transfer Service agents in parallel at Site B
choices.rationale: At 200 Mbps, even at full rated speed Site B needs many months, so parallel agents on the same link do not rescue it.

choices.text: Transfer Appliance for Site B only; Storage Transfer Service over the network for A and C
choices.rationale: Site B would take hundreds of days online, while A and C finish within about a day, so only B justifies an appliance.

explanation: Compare each site's online duration with the one-week guideline: only the huge, slow-linked site justifies shipping hardware.

prompt: Altostrat must move an 80 TB archive from a legacy on-premises NAS to Cloud Storage over its existing hybrid link. At the bandwidth the network team will allow, the transfer takes about three days, and the team wants managed retries, bandwidth control and integrity validation. Which approach fits?

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service with on-premises agents, with bandwidth limits and integrity validation
choices.rationale: Storage Transfer Service uses self-hosted agents for on-premises sources, with parallelism, automatic retries, bandwidth control and integrity validation.

choices.text: Order a Transfer Appliance, since archives larger than 50 TB should always be shipped
choices.rationale: An appliance is worth considering when an online upload would take over a week; here it takes about three days, and no 50 TB rule exists.

choices.text: Write a cron job on a jump host that runs a copy command and reruns it after failures
choices.rationale: Custom scripts lack managed scheduling, parallel agents, automatic retries and bandwidth control, so the team would build and own them.

choices.text: Use Datastream to replicate the NAS file changes continuously into a Cloud Storage bucket
choices.rationale: Datastream replicates database changes, not NAS file trees.

explanation: With a usable link and a short duration, online transfer through Storage Transfer Service agents beats shipping hardware or hand-rolled scripts.

prompt: A retailer follows the Google Cloud migration framework of assess, plan, deploy and optimize. The discovery inventory is complete, and the team is now in the plan phase. Which two activities belong in this phase? Choose two.

choices.text: Run discovery to build the application and environment inventory
choices.rationale: Building the inventory is the assess phase, which the team has already completed.

choices.text: Build the foundation: resource hierarchy, identity, projects and network design
choices.rationale: The plan phase builds the foundational infrastructure, including identity, project organization and networking.

choices.text: Execute the production cutover waves for each application group
choices.rationale: Moving workloads is the deploy phase.

choices.text: Choose a migration approach per workload, such as rehost or replatform
choices.rationale: Developing the migration strategy, including the migration type for each workload, is part of the plan phase.

choices.text: Tune performance and cost using cloud-native services after workloads land
choices.rationale: Leveraging cloud-native capabilities to improve performance and cost is the optimize phase.

explanation: Assess inventories, plan builds the foundation and decides strategy, deploy moves workloads, optimize improves them afterwards.

prompt: A company has twelve Tomcat-based Java applications on VMware VMs. The original developers have left, so source changes are risky, but leadership wants the applications on GKE to standardize on containers. Which approach fits best?

choices.text: Use Migrate to Containers to run a fit assessment and generate container artifacts
choices.rationale: Migrate to Containers converts VM workloads, including Tomcat applications on VMware, into containers for GKE with a guided fit assessment and no rewrite.

choices.text: Use Migrate to Virtual Machines and keep the applications as Compute Engine VMs
choices.rationale: This rehosts the VMs but does not meet leadership's goal of running on GKE.

choices.text: Rebuild each application as new stateless microservices running on Cloud Run
choices.rationale: A rebuild needs deep source changes, which is the risk the team wants to avoid.

choices.text: Move the VMs to VMware Engine, which converts them into containers automatically
choices.rationale: VMware Engine runs the VMware stack as it is and does not convert VMs into containers.

explanation: When the goal is containers without source rewrites, replatform with Migrate to Containers after a technical fit assessment.

prompt: A hospital network's data center lease ends in five months. It runs 1,500 vSphere VMs governed by NSX policies and custom backup tooling, managed by VMware-skilled operators. Applications cannot be modified, and the team wants networking, security policy and operational tooling to stay unchanged during the move, with modernization later. Which target fits best?

choices.text: Compute Engine via Migrate to Virtual Machines, rebuilding each VM's network policy
choices.rationale: This changes the hypervisor, networking constructs and tooling, which the team wants to keep unchanged during the move.

choices.text: GKE, using Migrate to Containers to containerize each VM into a new image set
choices.rationale: Containerization is a replatforming effort per application and violates the no-modification and unchanged-tooling constraints.

choices.text: VMware Engine, keeping vSphere, NSX and HCX-based tooling and policies as they are
choices.rationale: VMware Engine runs the VMware platform on dedicated Google bare metal, letting teams reuse existing tools, skills and policies and defer modernization.

choices.text: Cloud Run, after refactoring each application into small stateless services
choices.rationale: Refactoring contradicts the no-modification constraint and cannot fit a five-month deadline.

explanation: When tooling, policy and skills must stay unchanged and applications cannot change, VMware Engine is the lowest-friction destination. Modernize later.

prompt: A bank has a 90-application portfolio and an aggressive deadline. The program lead wants the first migration wave to build team confidence and validate the landing zone, in line with gradual rollouts and proof-of-concept validation. Which two applications make the best first wave? Choose two.

choices.text: An internal wiki with few dependencies that can tolerate a weekend outage
choices.rationale: Low dependencies and tolerance for downtime make it easy to migrate and roll back, ideal for validating the foundation.

choices.text: The core payments ledger, because migrating the riskiest system first surfaces problems early
choices.rationale: A high-risk, high-impact system is a poor pilot; guidance favors small initial rollouts that limit the blast radius.

choices.text: A customer-facing mobile backend with a five-nines SLO and many upstream integrations
choices.rationale: Near-zero downtime and many dependencies make it among the hardest to migrate and unsuitable for a confidence-building first wave.

choices.text: A mainframe settlement system with no supported VM or container path
choices.rationale: Without a supported migration path it needs a specialized plan, which is not a quick win.

choices.text: A batch reporting tool with a documented rollback and no real-time dependencies
choices.rationale: A self-contained batch workload with a tested rollback is easy to validate, and a failure would have limited impact.

explanation: Early waves should be low-risk and low-dependency, with tolerance for downtime and a rehearsed rollback.

prompt: A team is writing the runbook for a weekend database and VM cutover. Which three practices are consistent with Google Cloud migration guidance? Choose three.

choices.text: Lower DNS record TTLs to a minimum ahead of the cutover so traffic can be redirected quickly
choices.rationale: Setting DNS TTLs to the minimum before migrating allows faster traffic redirection, including during a rollback.

choices.text: Delete the source environment right after cutover so that split-brain writes can never occur there
choices.rationale: Removing the source immediately removes the rollback path; keep it until the migration is validated.

choices.text: Define a rollback step and a maximum execution time for each step, then rehearse them
choices.rationale: Guidance is to prepare a rollback strategy for every step, set a maximum execution time, and test the strategies regularly.

choices.text: Skip rollback rehearsal for steps already proven in the pilot, to save time in the weekend window
choices.rationale: Rollback strategies should be tested regularly rather than assumed, and pilots do not cover the production cutover context.

choices.text: Keep a backup access path, such as internet access, while changing interconnect settings
choices.rationale: Backup channels prevent lockout if a connectivity change goes wrong.

explanation: A good cutover runbook has fast traffic redirection, per-step rollback with time limits, and a backup access path.

prompt: An order database accepts writes around the clock, and the business can tolerate only a few minutes of downtime at cutover. Which Database Migration Service job type should be used to move it to Cloud SQL?

choices.text: One-time, which takes a snapshot of the database at a single point in time
choices.rationale: A one-time job copies a point-in-time snapshot, so every write after it would be missing at cutover.

choices.text: Continuous, but only after all writes are stopped so the initial load is consistent
choices.rationale: Continuous jobs migrate data while the source stays operational, and stopping writes for the full load would create long downtime.

choices.text: Continuous, which does an initial dump and load and then streams ongoing changes
choices.rationale: Continuous migration follows the initial full dump with a flow of changes until cutover, minimizing downtime.

choices.text: One-time, scheduled again every night until the cutover weekend
choices.rationale: Repeated snapshots still leave a gap of up to a day, and each run is a full copy instead of a stream of changes.

explanation: Low-downtime database moves use continuous jobs: initial load, then change data capture, then a short cutover.

prompt: A company stores 150 TiB of image assets in Amazon S3 and must copy them into Cloud Storage, then keep the bucket in sync until the application cutover. The team does not want to provision or operate any transfer hosts. Which service fits?

choices.text: Transfer Appliance, shipped to the AWS region to copy the data and returned to Google
choices.rationale: Transfer Appliance is for moving data from your own locations; it is not used to extract data from another cloud's object store.

choices.text: Migrate to Virtual Machines with an AWS source, replicating the S3 data as a VM disk
choices.rationale: Migrate to Virtual Machines replicates AWS virtual machines, not object storage.

choices.text: Storage Transfer Service with Amazon S3 as the source and a recurring schedule
choices.rationale: Storage Transfer Service supports S3 as a source with scheduling; agents are required only for on-premises sources, so no transfer hosts are needed.

choices.text: Database Migration Service with a continuous job reading the bucket contents
choices.rationale: Database Migration Service moves relational databases, not object data.

explanation: Cloud-to-cloud object copies are Storage Transfer Service territory: agentless for S3 sources, schedulable, and parallelized.
